JAZZ ON JAZZ \ J A SASS -Anita Baker (1) stopped backstage to meet Sarah Vaughan at New York's Blue Note, where the Divine One was recently in residence. L ots of leftover STUFF - It's too early in the year to get analytical and in- cisive, so let's just clean off the desk: First off, last issue I published my list of the 10 best jazz albums of '87. It wasn't an easy list to compile, but I'd just like to men- tion the artists whose albums almost made the list (the runners-up, as it were). In no particular order: Michel Petrucciani, The Sonny Clark Memorial Quartet, Tim Berne, Dave McKenna, Dave Hol- land, Marvin "Smitty" Smith, several Steve Lacy projects (a couple with Mai Waldron, some other duets, another Sextet album or two), George Adams/Don Pullen, Joe Williams, Shirley Horn, Ray Anderson, Mose Allison, Charlie Haden, Major Holley/Slam Stewart and Mike Westbrook. As usual, I didn't include reissues or previously-unissued items (there'd be too many and it's unfair for con- temporary records to be compared to reissued masterpieces) or such non-jazz items as the new records by Joao Gilberto and Caetano Veloso... WoJ/ Trap Salutes Dizzy Gillespie: An All-Star Salute to tl^ ]azz Master will be aired around February 26 over most PBS Stations, as part of the new season of Great Performances. The 90-minute show - culled from a fantastic 70th birthday tribute to the great Diz taped at Wolf Trap last year - will feature the baron of bebop in numerous settings, including per- formances with the likes of Sonny Rollins, Wynton Marsalis and Car- men McRae.. ..Virgin Records is get- ting set to unveil Venture Records, an - are you ready? - "adventure across the boundaries of music". Well, we'll see about that, but among those with debut Venture releases due in Feburary are Lester Bowie's Brass Fantasy and England's Itchy Fingers. ..The Na- tional Academy of Jazz has in- ducted Barry Manilow into its Board of Governors - a worthwile choice, goodness knows. ..In the up- coming (figure Christmas of '88) film Scrooge (just what we need, another screen version of The Christmas Carol), starring Bill Mur- ray, there's a scene in which Miles Davis, David Sanborn, Larry Carlton and Paul Shaffer appear as street musicians. Ho, ho. ho.. .Singers & The Song, Gene Lee's account of popular (read: Sinatra, Sarah, Peggy Lee, etc.) singers has recently been published ($18.95, Oxford University Press). ..GRP Records has signed Japan's Yutaka (a koto and synthesizer player), Hungary' s Szacksi (a pianist), and Americans John Patittucci (a bas- sist) and Eric Marienthal (a saxophonist) to record deals. If the last two sound familiar, they're in Chick Corea's current band, and oT Chick is producing the records.. .Look, vinyl lives. Since just about every jazz reissue this day is coming out on CD only, it's almost surprising to see that Atlan- tic, anyway, is still reissuing jazz on vinyl. New in the Jazzlore series are Big Joe Turner's 1956-59 "Big Joe Rides Again" (a jazz album with, among others, Coleman Hawkins, Lawrence Brown and Pete Brown), 'The Art Farmer Quartet Featuring Jim Hall Live at the Half Note" ('63), the Modem Jazz Quartet's 1962 "Lonely Woman," Esther Phillips' "Confessin' The Blues" (a '66 big band date and a '70 small group date), Charles Mingus's wonderful "Oh Yeah" ('61), Lee Konitz's fine "Inside Hi-Fi" (two '56 quartet sessions), and Jess Stacy's "A Tribute to Benny Good- man," '54 sides done with Good- man sidemen and released to coin- cide with the Goodman screen biog- raphy. .Jazz From the City, a weekly two-hour contemporary jazz radio show hosted by Ken Webb, is now available via United Stations Satel- lite. Call (212) 401-1236 for the low- down...Antilles New Directions has just reissued saxophonist Jim Pepper's "Cornin' and Coin'," a well-named album that has, in a few years, been on Europa, Rykodisc and Antilles. ..Photog- rapher Joe La Russo has put out a limited edition poster of Woody Herman to benefit the National Academy of Jazz's Woody Herman Foundation Fund. The poster is available for $20 (unsigned) or $30 (signed) from La Russo Photog- raphy, PO Box 480357, Dept. BB, Los Angeles, CA 90048. ..Billy Taylor, Art Blakey and Lionel Hampton are the recipients of the National Endowment for the Arts' 1988 Jazz Masters Fellowships. The Fellow- ships carry $20,000 grants. ..GRP toured a good hunk of its artist roster in Japan in October, "GRP Super Live '87," and expect to see live albums, videos, and all sorts of other stuff from the tour early this year...NEWJAZ-TV is a new service that broadcasts new age and jazz album cover art videos (trust me) unscrambled, for free, to cable sys- tems. Want to know more? Call them in Fort Collins, CO at (303) 484-5535 and they'll tell you more.. .Next week I'll get incisive and analytical (about various boxed sets, OJCs, OBCs, and more). ON JAZZ D JAZZ - With all the reis- suing going on - with all the oddball collectors items that are now being digitally-remastered and brought back into circulation - you'd as- sume that all the essential jazz records are available, that all the really important artists are well rep- resented by American product. You'd be wrong. The must-have Charlie Parker Dial sides, for ex- ample, are, for the most part, out-of- print stateside, be it on CD, vinyl, whatever. One absolutely essential jazz art- ist who has always been poorly-rep- resented by American issues is Django Reinhardt, the gypsy guitar genius who remains the most important non-American jazz musician of all time. Since he primarily recorded for European labels, the cream of Django's work (which is the cream of his work with The Quintet of the Hot Club of France, which he co-led with Stephane Grappelli) has been available largely as imports. Not anymore. DRG, bless their reissuing little hearts, has (under their Disques Swing imprint) brought out the first set in a well- known French series called Djan- gologie, a series that, when the dust settles, will include 24-LPs worth of Django material. The first set, which covers the years 1928-40, is out now in a seven-LP boxed set (complete with a booklet detailing Django's entire discography). Next month most of the first set (every- thing but an LPs worth of miscel- laneous sides Django recorded with various vocalists) will be out in two two-CD sets. Django Reinhardt remains one of the most influential jazz guitarists of all time - his style, his sound (an instantly recognizable acoustic guitar sound falling somewhere be- tween the sound of a guitar and the sound of a zither), and the brilliant- ly charming music he made with the Quintet of the Hot Club (his spiky guitar beautifully com- plementing Grappelli's liquid violin, over the distinctive Gallic churning of two rhythm guitars and bass) were all the work of a com- plete original. This first set - drawn, mainly, from the recordings Reinhardt did for the Pathe label - includes most of the pre-War Hot Club sides (Grappelli spent the War in London while Reinhardt remained in Paris, virtually ending their working relationship), and some wonderful recordings with the likes of Eddie South, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Bill Coleman and Rex Stewart. Throughout Reinhardt is casually thrilling - tossing off mer- curial improvisations with the kind of relaxed, easy grace unheard of in all but the very finest jazz players. It's time now to reevaluate the great Django Reinhardt, who, some 35 years after his death, remains as influential, and as breathtakinj original, as any jazz artist of generation. The first set of Djan- gologie is a superb place to start. PASSING ON - 1 was quite sad- dened, upon returning from Christmas vacation, to hear of the sudden death in December of tenor saxophonist Warne Marsh. Marsh was a somewhat hard-to-pin-down player - he spent a lot of time teach- ing and a lot of time living and working outside of the usual jazz centers - but he was always a joy to hear. His dry tenor saxophone - what Lester Young might have sounded like if he studied with Len- nie Tristano - will be missed, as will his always delightful pairings with fellow-Tristanoite Lee Konitz. Warne Marsh was 60. LANDMARK ACCORD - Orrin Keep- news (l), president of Landmark Records, and Larry Rosen, co-president of GRP, grin it up as they celebrate the deal by which GRP will distribute Landmark product in Europe. OB&JCs - Fantasy quietly put out another stack of midline jazz reissues before the holidays, slip- ping in a set of blues reissues for ood measure. Under the Original azz Classics heading are 30 jazz reissues (all but nine also on CD) from the likes of Monk, Coltrane, Tyner, Rollins and Ammons (in- cluding the first OJC reissues from the Milestone label). Under the Original Blues Classics heading (the second issue under that name, the first since 1984) are 15 albums (no CDs on these) by the likes of Mem- phis Slim, Rev. Gary Davis, Alber- ta Hunter, Blind Willie McTell and Tampa Red. Good stuff, no matter how you slice it, BY GEORGE - Teledisc (you know, those people who put out those records they hawk on TV at night) has just put out a fine pack- 1 mwh age. The Gershwin Collection, to honor the 50th anniversary of the death of George Gershwin. What makes the set (53 songs on four LPs or cassettes, $29.95, and three CDs, $39.95) so unusual is the range of ar- tists represented. From Gershwin himself through A1 Jolson and Judy Garland to Billie Holiday and Art Tatum to Willie Nelson and Bob Hope to the N.Y. Philharmonic and London Symphony, this is an effec- tively prismatic look at one man's music. Call (800) 543-5400 to order. Anyway, this is it, the news flashes . . . the hot items . . . the inside stuff culled from press releases, phone calls, album jackets, gum wrappers, paid informers, letters, postcards and the bathroom walls at Music+. Let’s start by introducing ourselves. I am a facilitator, my purpose is to serve the independent industry in any way I can. That means you have to tell me what you need; and we have to talk. Often. I am far more capable of error than my mother says I am. Your guidance and assistance are invaluable. In late December, pouring over 12 months worth of charts in an attempt to analyze the presence of in- dependent productfor the Cash Box year-end issue, I made a supe- rior goofby somehow eliminating Clarence Carter’s Doctor C.C. album which was visible for months on the Black Contemporary charts. Thank you, Ichiban, for understanding. The Doctor is now in. On with it. Good evening Mister and Mrs. America and all the ships at sea . . . lets go to press. Item: William G. Stilfield has formed a new label, CHASE MUSIC GROUP (CMG), and has begun releasing jazz and blues product. In fact, they have already enjoyed exhilarating sales successes with their CD issues ofTom Grant’s Heart of the City and John Lee Hooker’s Jealous, the latter being currently sold-out. Item: Jennifer Lynne of Newstar Records (Toledo, OH) writes to tell us of company president Michael Drew Shaw’s new album project, Moonshine, which is scheduled for release in early March. Shaw’s pre- vious releases include “Pigskin Widow” and on a more serious note “Distant Shores (We Will Go On)” which reflects on the Challenger shuttle tragedy and is performed by students from the Concord, N.H. high school where Christa McAuliffe taught. Apparently Shaw is an aggressive marketing person, as all his efforts receive good local coverage and support. Like all independent labels, Newstar’s main problem is airplay . . . c’mon you music directors and pds, give a lit- tle listen. Item: James T. Price of Sun-Ray Records in Lexington, KY is look- ing for a listing of country music stations across the U.S.A., and some tips on getting airplay for his release of “Road Blocks To Your Heart” backed with “My Angel Just Lost Her Wings” sung by Bud Chowning. Listening copies are available to interested radio folks and record dis- tributors by contacting Jim at (606) 254-7474. Item: Does anyone know anything about the FIRST URBAN GOLD RAP MUSIC AWARDS SHOW AND BENEFIT? I was gonna hip, hop down there, but no one returned my phone call. Help. Item: Fantasy has released a whole rackful of vintage jazz CDs on the Original Jazz Classics label, including Coleman Hawkin’s 1959 album, Hawk Eyes and Chet Baker Sings which, by the way, fea- tures some of my personal song favorites like “How Long Has This Been Going On?.” Fifteen CD titles to choose from ... a fun time for those of us who cut our jazz teeth on Sonny Rollins, McCoy Tyner, Milt Jackson and etc. Item: KAM-EXECUTIVE label president Butch Kelly drops a line from Charlotte. N.C. to let us know he has recently released a new gospel 45 by LeBo Blackmon, ‘The Lord’s Been Good To Me,” backed with, “Call On Jesus.” The label has expanded its roster to include the dance-rap act L.A. Stars, and should be releasing their first single soon. Tim Green, who wrote “Party Freak” for Ca$hflow, is providing the songs, so we’ll be expecting big things from this one. Item: Hot LA guitarist Andy Stroud, formerly with Toe Jam and Jam Demand has been earning a wide reputation for his ability to work in diverse music categories . . . he’s on the new Run DMC album . . . plays explosive funk/jazz fusion in live appearances . . . even gave out with some down home licks in helping a friend with some country music demos . . . look for him to be back at the Roxy and Whiskey later this year. Item: Scouting around LA? Take a listen to Disposable Income, playing at an unlikely neighborhood tavern on Fountain and Norman- die Friday and Saturday nights. If you don’t like the band you can al- ways get in some 8-ball. Warning: if you drink anything more exotic than scotch and water, this bar may not be for you. ’Bye for now. I’m going to Carolina in my mind. Stay indie groove. Phyllis J. Wickham ash Box January 23. 1988 19

JAZZ ON JAZZ 7 P ' ASSING ON - Joe Albany, the bebop pianist who recorded with Charlie Parker, Lester Young and I many others, died January 12 in New York of upper respiratory failure and cardiac arrest, bringing to an end one of the strangest careers in jazz. For most of his career, Joe Albany was the prototypical jazz junkie - spending a lot of time in jail for drugs, petty thievery, pimping, things like that. Every once in awhile, he'd pop up t for a minute or two - surfacing in the late-'50s to record a Riverside » album with Warne Marsh (who also died recently). The Right Com- bimtion. The album got positive , reviews, but Albany was unable to cash in on it - he was still off the scene. This led to him forever being tagged as "legendary," because nobody could find him. Then he surfaced in Europe in the early-'70s and, finally, returned to New York in 1979, where he played clubs, recorded (for Elektra/Musician most notably), got lots of press * coverage, was the subject of a film documentary, Joe Albany, A Jazz Life, .and, in generi, seemed to be back on the scene to stay. Joe Albany sounded better than ever - playing bebop with a confident fizz. But then - at the height of his comeback ~ Joe Albany suffered an aneurysm in the brain and slipped back into , obscurity. He surfaced every now and again, but he was finish^. Joe Albany was 63. And Ray Bauduc, a Swing Era drummer who worked most notab- ly with Bob Crosby's Bobcats, died ‘ January 8 in Houston Texas at the ^ age of 81. TRAVEL-LOGUE - Allan Botschinksy (1) and Nids-Henning Oersted Pedersen play- ing a recent engagement at N.Y.C.'s Village Gate, in support of their new album. Duologue (JAA. Music). CDCn - Epic Record s is about to issue its third set of CDs drawn from the CTI catalogue (they issued 14 titles last April and 13 titles in November). The fact that these are only coming out on CDs allows Epic - which, with the exception of ' ' the CD of Bad seems to be following the general CBS policy of not adding , extra tracks to the CDs - to beef up the discs with extra tracks, alternate takes, all sorts of stuff. Anyway, ex- pect more about this in the near fu- ture, and expect Hubert Laws' Crying Song, George Benson's Bad Benson, Airto's Free, Ron Carter's Yellow 6* Green, Joe Farrell's Moon Germs, Deodato 2, Jackie & Roy's Time & Love, Freddie Hubbard's R£ep Your Soul Together, The N.Y. Jazz Quartet's In Concert in Japan, Volume 1, Esther Phillips' From a Whisper to a Scream, Stanley Turrentine's Cherry, and a sampler, to show up in stores any minute (if they're not there already). CTTs Creed Taylor was a sound man -- CTI LPs always sounded terrific - and that care pays off on these bright, clear CDs. Epic, by the way, is truly about to make themselves a jazz force again, turning the Portrait imprint into a label for jazz, cabaret music, per- haps other alternate forms of musi- cal expression. Sade and Cyndi Lauper, who've been recording on the Portrait label, will now be under the Epic umbrella, clearing the Portrait name for the jazz stuff. More on this, too, at a later date. BOPPING AROUND- Bertrand Tavernier, the director of Round Midnight, has turned as far away from jazz as he could for his follow- up, or so it would seem. Beatrice is a film about incest, rape and plunder in the Middle Ages and it's an awful film - it's like a two-hour headache. However, the film's score was written and played by bassist Ron Carter, who was in Round Midnight. The score doesn't quite fit, but it certainly doesn't hurt any...I should write something here commenting on the nominations for the Grammy Awards, but 1 won't. I'd rather just ignore the Grammy Award jazz nominations, which are as astute as ever...Hip Hub: Boston has just doled out something called the first annual Reverend Dr. Mar- rin Luther King Music Awards, to Boston natives who have made some "contribution to the music in- dustry," and, so honored this first time around, were Jaki Byard, Roy Haynes, Sabby Lewis, Mae Arnett, and Donna Summer.. .Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs had dug out several new jazz CD releases. From Robert Parker's astonishing "Great Original Perrformances of Jazz Classics in Digitial Stereo," come CDs of Johnny Dodds 1923-29 and Jelly Roll Morton - you've really never heard these two early jazz masters sound this good. And, from the vaults of Columbia Records, comes a CD of Blue Rose, Duke Ellington's excellent 1956 collaboration with Rosemary Clooney...Last week, it should be noted, was the SOth anniversary of Benny Goodman's landmark 1938 Carnegie Hall concert - which brought swing to the concert haU - and Bob Wilber led a nifty re-crea- tion of the concert at Carnegie. AND THE NOMINEES ARE...-Current Grammy nominees Janice Siegel and Branford Marsalis were two of the record biz luminaries who announced some of this year’s Grammy nominees during the New York press con- ference at the Parker-Meridien Hotel.. Revolution (Continued from page 4) publicity,"There's a very strong in- terest in music from different parts of the world, and it's an interest that goes beyond esoteric folk music, or ethnomusicological interest in obscure exotica. In short, people are interested in pop. Music that was not meant to be appreciated in a scholar- ly or esoteric way; music to dance to, music to be excited by, just like you'd be excited by any other pop music." To develop this audience Shanachie will be providing divider cards for retailers, full color posters, and other promotional items in order to create a well defined new world beat sec- tion within retail outlets. Grass speaks of flourishing world beat scenes in San Francisco, New York, Austin, and England, where several record labels have banned together under the world beat banner to coor- dinate marketing efforts. Much of the world beat scheduled to be released has been available as high priced imports in the past, and will be available domestically through licensing agreements. Shanachie will issue several records that have appeared on Britain's Globestyle Records, including an ex- cellent collection of rocking accor- dian music from Columbia entitled Fiesta Vallenata. Grass points out that whenever possible Shanachie has licensed music from the original ar- tists or producers. Shanachie also hopes to intiate recording projects in the future. Celluloid's Braziloid catalogue is owned in Brazil by Brazilian RCA, and comes to America through an agreement which essentially allows RCA to issue Celluloid Afro-pop LPs in Brazil while Braziliod issues RCA's Brazilian records in the U.S. The core of the Braziloid catalogue^ lies in the current work of established ^ *' stars like Gilberto Gil and Maria x Bethania, but the label will also be taking chances with new Brazilian rock and pop bands like Obina Shock ^ and Lobao, as well as Martinho Da^^ Vila's neo-traditional pagode. The ^ Braziloid sampler will be available. the first week in Febuary, and in- cludes "Vida" by Obina Shock, a hit ' - from 1987 that has the sound of Zairian guitar pop over disco drum- ming and features guest vocals by^^ Gilberto Gil and Gal Costa. Celluloid reports the song garnered some col-^ lege airplay in California when released on a promo cassette. - ^ PolyGram's Best Of Brazil series will feature greatest hits packages of 60s and 70s material by estabhshed-fj-r - Brazilian stars like Gilberto Gil, Caetano Veloso, Ellis Regina, and Gal Costa all of which have been avail- able from Brazilian PolyGram. A record of new material by Velosa is set for March 21, as is a record of American jazz standards sung bossa nova style by Nara Leao. That same month CBS will be releasing the new Milton Nascimento record, which'" features vocals by Paul Simon. v Virgin's Earthworks series will be issuing records already available in England. Thunder Before Dawn (The Indestructible Beat Of Soweto, Volume 2) is a companion to the sampler of township jive released by Shanachie in the summer of 1986. A full LP by ^ the great "groaner" of township jive, • -- Simon "Mahlathini" Nkabinde, is ^ also set for release, as are the collec- tions Hurricane Zouk and Heartbeat Soukous. S ONY DAYS - Sony Cor- poration of America has begun something called the Sony Innovators Program which, the press release says, is to recognize "up-and-coming black artists in film, television and music." '^e're interested in joining with the entertainment industry in recognizing not only excellence but ^also innovative creative expres- sion," says Neil Vander Ehissen, president of Sony Corporation of “America. "It's our wish that the Sony Irmovators Program features artists who demonstrate unique qualities in their work - artists who aren't afraid of trying new things and testing old limits. These per- formers will deserve to reach great 'heights in their careers. We just want to help them get their first taste of recognition." The way this works is three judges select groups of finalists from those nominated by record compani^, and then a hotshot art- •ist gets to choose who gets the honor. Does this make sense? Anyway, Herbie Hancock (who - coincidentally? - records for Sony- owned CBS Records) chose Terence Blanchard and Donald Harrison twho ” coincidentally? - record for the same label) and Quincy Jones chose Al. B. Sure! (a vocalist/producer/arranger) and everybody got their awards and pats-on-the-back last week. PASSING ON - Al Hall, a veteran jazz bassist, died January 18 in New York City. Hall was one of Ihose guys who backed everybody - he was a popular accompanist with all manner of jazz artists, and he was also a familiar figure in Broadway pit orchestras. He was 72 JAZZ 88 IN '88 - WBGO-FM, »New York's (via Newark, New Jer- sey) 24-hour jazz station has more listeners than any other public radio station in the U.S., according to the latest Arbitron figures. That chalks up at 360,700 listeners per week. That's a lot of listeners. And th^ play jazz, folks, only jazz. Other stuff about 'BGO: They've got a whole slate of Black History Month events coming up and they're co- sponsoring a Mardi Gras celebra- tion at the Market at the Citicorp Building in Manhattan, Febrary 24- 27, with performances by Harry Connick Jr., Loren Schoenberg, Irene Reid, and a host of others. IN THE GROVE - The Grove School of Music, located in Studio City, CA, will begin a jazz-oriented "Professional Instrumental Program" this fall and the excellent Canadian big band leader, Rob Mc- Connell, will be moving south to serve as its supervising instructor. McConnell will conduct a cross- country audition tour in advance of the fall, and (818) 985-0905 is the number to call for details. WOODY 'N' RICHARD - Richard Stoltman will lead the Woody Herman ghost band, under the direction of Frank Tiberi, at a February 13 Carnegie Hall concert, part of a national tour in support of Ebony Concerto, the due-any-day RCA Red Seal album featuring the classical clarinetist and the Herman Herd. TO THE MAX - Max Roach, who - goodness knows - has never shied away from new challenges, will be joining Kodo, the renowned Japanese percussion troup, on March 8 at New York's City Center in a piece called "Macrame." Kodo will be on an 11-week tour, but this collaboration with Max Roach will be a one-time-only affeir. EPIC, TWO - Last week I men- tioned something about Epic's Portrait imprint beginning to move in a jazz direction and right after deadline some of the details floated by my desk: Don Grierson, E/Ps senior vp ofA&R, willnm the show, Andy Fuhrman, Epic's A&R direc- tor, will oversee the "day-to-day operations" of the label, and the first signings include Ornette Coleman and Prime Time and David Murray. Those are two very hip signings. Very, very hip sign- ings. And Portrait will iso reissue historic material under the 'Tortrait Legends" logo. One more label in the pool. Splash! ON JAZZ B etty - "l recorded for record labels, but there was really hardly any promo- tion," says Betty Carter, who, since 1970, has put her records out on her own Bet-Car label. "What record companies tend to do about jazz is that, if the market says that jazz is only one percent or ten percent or three percent or five per- cent of the business, this is all that they seem to put their initiative in. 'Okay, we're going to sell 10,000 records, so let's just put out 10,000 records.' "I still think there is a wider market out there for jazz, but I think that the record companies just tend, to lean over and deal with the per- centage that they've been going with all these years. So that is the problem - if you sell a record, the record company will just put the record out there; and if it doesn't sell, then that's the end of it. But I think that, like they do in the pop field, they should put more into it. I think that we would develop a much wider market for jazz. Be- cause I think that the time is really right for a new audience." The time, it would seem, is really right for Betty Carter. One of our very best jazz singers -- indeed, one of the very few bonafide jazz singers - Betty Carter is about to put out her first major label album in years. Verve will release a new Betty Carter album in the spring and, on top of that, will issue all the Bet-Car albums and there are some mighty fine Bet-Car albums - in all thr^ formats. To date, Bet- Car has been a vinyl-only opera- tion. Besides her prowess as a vocalist “ and there is nothing in jazz quite like the sight and sound of &tty Carter singing herself into a corner on a standard, reinterpreting the lyrics so that you hear a song you've Imown all your life and hear ironies where there were never ironies before -• Betty Carter has been one of the most eloquent drum-beaters for jazz. She sits on panels, she makes speeches, she has been very vocal in her opinion about what is jazz, what isn't jazz, and what's happening in this art form. "Well, Wynton's taken over for me now, he's doing it now. And the thing about him doing it is he's a man and he's a classical person, which gains a lot of respect. And he's young. And when young people see a young person telling them this or that, they seem to be more affected by that. I thought that the young people seeing me with young people playing with me would help. And it does help. But with Wynton, with the kind of press he's been getting, he's been really effective in getting a lot of young black kids interested in the music. Because that's really what Tm inter- ested in dealing with: gettingyoung black kids interested in this music. "The white colleges -- the large colleges - have brought us to their colleges. In the black colleges, we have not had the chance to really get down there and sell, sell, sell, sell this music like we should. And when we do bring this music to the black colleges, we bring down a bunch of old fuddy-duddies. And young kids are not interested in looking at old fuddy-duddies, the think it's old-time music. So if they brought a bunch of young kids down there, their peers, I think it would be more effective. So now that Wynton's doing it. I'll just let him do that. And I'll stdl continue to do my thing, because it's all about the culture, it's all ab(3ut black cul- ture. I want to make these young kids realize that it was the black people who started this wonderful music of jazz, and not Dave Brubeck. 'Tn fact, I was in Ann Arbor recently and there was a group of young black kids who came to seem me. And one of the students asked me, “Why are there more white Another project that should see the light of a record release this year is a very unusual meeting of a pair of jazz divas. Betty Carter and Car- men McRae recorded together live at San Francisco's Great American Music Flail, but the release of the record has been held up due to some legal wrangling. Betty is con- fident that it will be sorted out soon, and this unique item - which she says is "very, very, veiy good. Very interesting and very good" ^ will hit the streets. "They've got to market jazz, they've got to do better," says Betty Carter about the record company powers that be. 'T hope I can in- spire PolyGram and Verve, I hope I can have a real affect on their marketing side of the business. The companies can just promote the ar- tists they get a little better. And they can get good artists, young good ar- tists who have the enthusiasm, the inspiration, the love for the music, so that they won't have to defect later on. IJa them stay m the busi- ness a little longer, so they can just improve on their art, get better and better, and not have to say, 'Well, nothing's happening to me, so I guess I'll just go over and get a hit record and be unhappy' 'T don't want that to happen." NEWS EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE Due to a printer's error, last week's On Jazz column was incorrect. This week we have two columns - below and on page 21. We apologize for any inconvenience. ON JAZZ 4 80! - Stephane Grappelli (c), who'll be the subject of an 80th birthday concert celebra- tion, April 14 at Carnegie Hall, with Ettore Stratta (r) and Pat Phillips, whose new Stratta/Phillips Productions Inc. will coor- dinate the event. P ASSING ON - Richard Bock, founder of the Pacific Jazz and World Pacific record labels, and a longtime west coast producer, died February 5 of a heart attack at the age of 61. Pacific Jazz recorded such artists as Buddy Rich, Geny Mulligan, Gerald Wilson, Chet Baker, the Jazz Crusaders and Jean-Luc Ponty; it was an impor- tant label for the promotion of west coast jazz acts in the '50s and '60s. World Pacific was one of the first labels to try to forge a fusion be- tween jazz and Indian music (Ravi Shankar recorded for World Pacific years before George Harrison found him), a particular interest of Bock's, who was a founder of the S.A.I. Foundation, a non-profit foundation dedicated to the teach- ings of Bhagavan Sri Sathya Sai Baba. Of late, Bock has been producing a number of records for Fantasy's Contemporary label, in- cluding albums by Frank Morgan, Teny Gibbs/Buddy DeFranco and Bud Shank. Coincidentally, the Pacific Jazz and World Pacific labels are getting a new lease on life, with the intro- duction of "EMI-Manhattan Jazz Classics," a new CD-only midline imprint. Manhattan has steadfastly been reissuing Blue Notes for some time now, but has ignored the many other jazz holdings of the Capitol- EMI group, things like Pacific Jazz. Out not, from the Pacific catalogues, are The Immortal Clifford Brown, Gil Evans's New Bottle, Old Wine, Lambert, Hendricks & Ross's The Swingers, Gerry Mulligan/Chet Baker's Reunion, and Mulligan's California Concerts Volume One; com- ing in April are reissues of items by Mulligan, Lee Konitz, Annie Ross/Zoot Sims, Hoagy Car- michael, Jim Hall and Gil Evans (Great Jazz Standards). Gil Evans, by the way, will turn 75 in May. A couple of years ago, you would have been hard-pressed to find any Gil Evans albums in stores, but the past few months have seen a particular boom in Gil Evans reis- sues (almost all available only on CD). There are the two Pacific Jazz albums listed above. Out of the Cool (Impulse!), There Comes a Time (RCA), and The Individualism of Gil Evans. Of course, the great arranger has had many of his Miles Davis collaborations issued on CD over the past year, worked and recorded with Robbie Robertson and Sting last year, and has led his own high- sprited big band every Monday night at Sweet Basil, where they've done several live recordings for Gramavision (recently Evans has been ill and has been temporarily out of the Basil slot). There's also an album reteaming him with Helen Merrill, due in the spring from PolyGram's Emarcy. Gil Evans CD bins will be well-stocked on his birthday, probably the best present he could have hoped for. BOPPING AROUND - The Chameleon Music Group, a Southern California indie, has in- troduced a midline CD program, 'The Chameleon DISCovery," that includes a number of jazz items from the Vee-Jay catalogue. ..The 1988 Boston Globe Jazz & Heritage Festival gets the land of the bean and the cod hopping, March 10-20, with performances all around the town from the likes of Mel Torme, Carmen McRae, George Shearing, Lionel Hampton, The O'Jays, the Fabulous Thunderbirds and The Modern Jazz Quartet; there will also be a special showcase for local talent. Call (617) 523-6686 for more information. ..Delta Music, a West German classical music label that releases its product on CD, cassette and (gasp!) DAT, has begun a jazz and new age label called '7azzline." New Age guitarist Dagobert Boehm's Acoustic Moods is the first release...Mwendo Dawa, the popular (in Sweden) Swedish fusion group will play three quickie dates in New York; March 11 & 12 at the Jazz Center, March 19 at the United Nations' Dag Ham- marskjold Auditorium. ..Alice Tully Hall in New York will host a jazz evening as part of the annual "Composers' Showcase" series: The Mingus Dynasty (doing an un- recorded Mingus sketch). Sun Ra (doing a solo piano thing called "New York Town"), and Freddie Hubbard, Jon Hendricks, Joe Beck and others joining the Philhar- monia Virtuosi in the premiere of Charles Schwartz's jazz symphony, "Riding High." Schwartz is the founder of the series and I've found his jazz symphonies particularly uninteresting in the past. ..Vinyl- mania, a small independent record chain that practically owns the whole of Greenwich Village's Car- mine Street, has opened a jazz-only store at 30 Carmine. RUSSELL IS HERE-Singer- songwriter Brenda Russell calls her BRENDA RUSSELL Music began as a family affair for the Brooklyn, New York bom Brenda Gor- don. Her father was a professional singer who p>erformed for a time with the legendary Ink Spots; her mother was a singer-songwriter as well, and both parents encouraged Brenda's inter- est in music from her early childhood. Brenda's solo career began in 1979, when she recorded the acclaimed Bren- da Russell album featuring So Good, So Right, for Tommy LiPuma's A&M/Horizon LabeL A second A&M album. Love Life followed in 1981. When liPuma moved to Warner Bros Records, he quickly signed Brenda and produced her third album Two Eyes. Along the way, Russell's efforts were hardly confined to her solo recordings. She had also established an estimable reputation as a writer, with songs covered by Earth, Wind and Fire, Anne Murray, Roberta Flack and many others. She had also collaborated with Michael McDonald, Melissa Manchester and David Foster to name a few. Braida had also developed a solid standing as a s^ion singer, working with performers as diverse as Barbra Streisand, Elton John, Cher and Bette Midler, and as a backgroimd singer on the road with a host of top names. In 1984, Brenda recorded a fourth solo album in Stockholm, Sweden, where her previous Ips had been consistently suc- cessful. Although the album was never distributed in the United States, it laid the ^oundwork for Get Here. And with Get Here, Brenda Russell has delivered an album that promises to be very rewarding, indeed. JAZZ ON JAZZ P MANCINI, HENDRICKS & MANCINI - Jon Hendricks (1) recently vocalized at Santa Monica's The Loa to benefit the Society of Singers, which is presided over by Ginny I^ncini (e). That’s Henry Mancini (r) homing in on things. OLY DAYS- PolyGram Jazz has just put out another sparkling set of CD reissues from its vaults, almost , everything augmented by extra ^ material. Don Byas on Blue Star is the rarity o f the lot - 23 tracks by one of the greatest tenors of them all, all ^recorded on 78s for a small European label. Somewhat less rare, but no less worthwhile, are Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers' thunderous 1958 - Paris Olympia (from the Fontana catalogue), and, from Verve, Count Basie in London; Stan Getz Plays (particularly bril- '''^iiant early Verve Getz); the landmark The Individualism of Gil Evans, with enough extra tracks to nearly double the playing time of the LP; Bud Powell: Jazz Giant, and Bill Evans Alone. Prime stuff this, and the beginning of what should be a momentous year ofCD reissues from the folks at PolyGram Jazz. > PolyGram Jazz, as is now well known, has taken on distribution of the sister Black Saint and Soul Note labels, with PolyGram Special Im- ^ ports now just a memory. The Black Saint and Soul Note catalogue rep- resents the finest single contem- porary jazz label ~ Ital/s Giovanni "^Bonandrini has steadfastly recorded the artists on the cutting edge of jazz, along with some of the best of the bebop talent, winning the SJ^last four Down Beat Critics Polls for Label of the Year in the process. PSI I distributed all of these records < ..during the past few years: from the ' I big names to the little names. The J Black Saint and Soul Note catalogue numbers well over 200 items, and _ PSI had it all available. PolyGram Jazz, which hews closer to a "what- sells /what-doesn't sell" ethic, is going to distribute only selected ’items from the catalogue; their new catalogue lists just over 80 Black Saints and Soul Notes. The rest of ;he catalogue is, apparently, up for * grabs, if a distributor wants to take I on a label that's being picked over. , [ PolyGram Jazz, at the same time, is *!.:>also going to be distributing j Europe's much smaller Owl, Red, * Minor Music and JMT labels, drop- ping Sound Aspects from the PSI roster. MILES - It must be hard for people who don't know all that much about jazz to tmderstand the endless fascination with Miles Davis that jazz fans of every age have. Go hear his current band and you hear some okay trumpet-play- ing patched on to some very ordi- nary funk/fusion. Listen, Fantasy has just released the CD version of MzZes Davis: Chronicle - The Complete Prestige Recordings on eight CDs in a box with a $125 list price. Just lis- ten to any of this - drop the laser anywhere on these discs - and music that is so haunting, so pierc- ing, so brilliant, and so authentical- ly American will bum a hole into your brain. MUes Davis was one jazz genius, make no mistake about that, and this set - which covers everything between the Birth of the Cool and the Columbias (now also being reissued on CD) - is absolute- ly essential. A landmark CD pack- age! THEIR BUDDY - A Buddy Rich Scholarship Fund, for talented and needy dmm students, has been es- tablished at the NYU School of Music. NAT "KING" - Capitol has begun an extensive Nat Cole CD reissue program and that is, for the most part, good news. Cole, of course, recorded tons of schlock for Capitol - syrupy romantic stuff that has its place, as sympy romantic schlock always wiU. However, in this batch of syrup are a number of fine items - tilings like Just One of Those Things (And More), with charts by Billy May, and Love is the Thing (And More), with charts by Gordon Jenkins. And in this bach of syrup is one of my personal favorite al- bums, one of those albums that I'd tell Tower Pulse! that I'd cart away with me to a desert island. The album is After Midnight and it's released here as The Complete After Midnight Sessions. It's a simple, low-keyed jazz date, recorded in 1956, and it is glorious. Nat Cole on piano and vocals, John Collins on guitar, Charlie Harris on bass, Lee Young on dmms and Stuff Smith, Hany "Sweets" Edison, Juan Tizol and altoist Willie Smith playing solos and obligattos (not together - each track has five players only). The album is positively bewitching. And this reissue (the album's been out of print for a long time) has five additional tracks - two with Edison, one each with the other guys - that are just as delightful as the rest of the album. Pure magic. In a word: perfect. NEWS Ooh-Pop-A-Dah Dizzy Turns 70 With A Great Performance By Lee Jeske NEW YORK - Forget about textbooks, grainy old newsreels and crumbly bits of newspaper for a minute. It's black history month and, without too much trouble, we can uncover a living, breathing, ac- tive piece of black history in our midst, a true giant of Afro-American culture - John Birks "Dizzy" Gil- lespie of Cheraw, South Carolina. One of the dozen most important jazz figures of all time, I reckon, and a man who can be called "one of the true giants of 20th Century American music" without much fear of con- tradiction. That claim is made next week by noted jazz broadcaster Willis Con- over at the start of Wolf Trap Salutes Dizzy Gillespie: An All-Star Tribute To The Jazz Master, a 90-minute segment of PBS' Great Performances that celebrates the 70th birthday year of the great Diz. Gillespie turned 70 last October (quietly playing some col- lege in the midwest somewhere on the day itself); this special was taped at Wolf Trap last June. The concert was five-and-a-half hours long and was, without question, the greatest single tribute to a living jazz musician I've ever witnessed. The television '< "sion - generously spiked with old film clips - features only a teeny-weeny bit of the concert, but it does give a much-deserved hunk of national television time to a jazz figure of monumental propor- tions. Dizzy Gillespie, folks, is a giant. Gillespie is too often undervalued, something that is due, in part, to his longevity, his ebullient spirit and generosity, and the fact that his greatest innovations were tied in with Charlie Parker. If Parker was the "bop," Gillespie was the "be" in bebop, but Parker lived free and died, and Gillespie shook his ass, clowned aroiond and lived for, so far, 70 years. He wasn't weird and mysterious like Miles and Monk, wasn't wild and self-destructive like Parker, wasn't self-serious and pom- pous and outrageous. He's just plain Diz - quick to help out a young musician with an encouraging word or a pat on the tush, willing to take gigs anywhere anytime, happy to make fun of himself or anything else. He's also been careless about his bands - never managing to put together the kinds of razor-sharp units that, say. Art Blakey or Miles Da\ds were able to assemble. Nah, Dizzy Gillespie often just slaps together guys who are workmanlike players, but good foils for his unstop- pable schtick. The guys are some- times exceptional, but the sheer per- DIZZY GILLESPIE sonality of Gillespie overwhelms them. The show at Wolf Trap, and the Great Performances version of it, gives us the bebop, of course, but it also highlights Dizzy Gillespie's groimd- breaking role in the blending of latin rhythms into jazz, focuses attention on his marvelous big bands, gives us a taste of the man as general jazz mover and shaker. 'I'm sort of a teacher," says Gil- lespie. 'Tf you play trumpet in jazz, you're influenced by Dizzy," says Wynton Marsalis. If you play jazz, period, you're influenced by Dizzy Gillespie. The program gives us Wynton (a neo-bopper), J.J. Johnson (a bebop- per), and Benny Carter (a pre-bop- per) doing "Birks Works"; Dizzy, Steve Turre, Mongo Santamaria, Candido, Dave Valentin, David Amram, Jimmy Owens, Arnie Lawrence, Chris White, Ignacio Ber- roa, Nicky Marrero and Sam Rivers doing "Fiesta Mojo"; Flora Purim, Airto, Freddie Hubbard and others doing "Tanga"; six trumpets (Dizzy, Wynton, Fr^die, Owens, Jon Fad- dis, and Vaughn Nark) doing 'Tour de Force"; Dizzy, James Moody and Jon Hendricks scatting through a wild "Ooh-Pop-A-Dah"; Dizzy and Oscar Peterson dueting on "All The Things You Are"; Dizzy and Sonny Rollins (with Hank Jones, Mickey Roker and Rufus Reid) tearing up "Wheatleigh Hall"; and Dizzy and Carmen McRae dueting on 'This is the End of a Beautiful Friendship." And other little snippets - an isolated Moody solo, the famous clip of Gil- lespie and Parker doing "Hot House," a clip of Gillespie, Max Roach and Jimmy Carter doing "Salt Peanuts," lots of talk about Dizzy, lots of delightful old stills and film clips. The show, though, leaves out tons of stuff: particularly a bullish, all-star big band that Gillespie rehearsed meticulously for hours before the concert. There's more Dizzy and Oscar, more Dizzy and Sonny, more Dizzy and Carmen, more of every- thing. Those who taped the concert taped all the rehearsals (there were lots of rehearsals), taped the whole concert, taped lots of interviews. Some of the performances on the show are trimmed down - a solo gets killed here, a chorus gets removed there. But it's an important show. PBS, which serves up operas and bal- lets and symphonies by the platter- ful, generally ignores jazz. Dizzy Gillespie is an entertainer, but he's not serious enough for PBS. Jazz isn't classy enough for PBS. Jazz isn't art. So we welcome a special like this with open arms, of course, and hope it's not just the usual drop in the bucket. Back to Gillespie for a minute. Very few of the greatest jazz in- novators are still alive and even fewer are still active. There's Gil- lespie, Miles Davis, Roy Eldridge, Benny Carter, Lionel Flampton, a couple of others. Dizzy Gillespie's chops aren't what they used to be ~ on some nights they're strong (on this Wolf Trap show they're strong), on other nights they're weak - but the music he makes is vibrant, living music. He's an enormous figtire in American music; somebody who should be celebrated daily, not every 70 years. Where's his Kennedy Center Honor? Where was the kind of attention paid to his 70th birthday that is routinely paid to milestone ce#^ Iso I Me" I J birthdays of our living classical com- posers? Why didn't PBS air this spe- cial arormd the time of his birthday ^ rather than holding it for Black His-.^ tory Month? \ In any case, black history mean3^ jazz, of course, and it means Duke El- lington and Louis Armstrong and Lester Young and John Coltrane and Jelly Roll Morton and Charlie Park and all of the dead icons. But it also means John Birks "Dizzy" Gillespi and Miles Davis and Benny Cart^ ' and Roy Eldridge and Lionel Hampton and Ella Fitzgerald and other living, breathing, working icons. Wolf Trap Salutes Dizzy Gillespie: An All-Star Tribute To The Jazz Master airS February 26th over most PBS sta- tions. Gillespie's band is out there al- i most every day -at festivals, at clubs^ .X at concerts. His records are very t much in print, and his CD catalogu^uj is growing (the recent RCA /Bluebird i CD reissue of his '40s big band sidec-’ is particularly important). He's got a new record - Dizzy with strings - in the can. Last summer, he toured aV, the helm of a big band for the first time in ages, and the band smok This summer's there's talk of a Gil- lespie Afro-Cuban band tour. ^ There is history in the historyj books. And, sometimes, there is his- tory right in front of our eyes. "1 rS ^ Rap In 1987: Bigger And Deffer By Joe Levy This was the year that all the naysayers who thought of rap as a fad were finally silenced. Rap broke out of New York: the records showed fertile hip-hop scenes in Miami (home of 2 Live Crew and Luke Skywalker Records), Philly (home of Schooly D and Steady B), and L.A. (home of Ice T). Rap went gold: Salt- N-Pepa, Dana Dane, and Whoodini were certified by the RIAA last month. Rap went pop: LL Cool J muscled in on Barry White's territory with "I Need Love," and Salt-N- Pepa's 'Tush It" is currently #22 on the Cash Box Top 100 Singles Chart. No trend, no fad, and no sell-out, rap continues to grow, mutate, and bust up into the mainstream. The facts of rap and hip-hop cul- ture remain the same this past year as the year before, the year before that, and every year in the music's nine year recorded history (and decade plus performance history): rap was the most vital, relentlessly creative, innovative, self-renewing and modernist form of popular music. Rap was big business, so big busi- ness got into rap. Following the tri- umph of RUN-DMC, who made rap crossover a reality with "Walk This Way," and the platinum success of the Beastie Boys, you could hardly expect the major labels to ignore rap. JAZZ ON JAZZ P -JL 1 ASSING ON- A1 Cohn, the massively swinging tenor saxophonist and longtime partner of Zoot Sims, died of liver cancer on February 15. Jsohn and Sims were adherents of Lester Young, though they both developed highly personal, though similar, tenor sounds and styles. *rhey also both first came to fame with the Woody Herman bands of the late-'40s. Cohn, aside from his steadfast mainstream tenor work, ^^as a talented writer and arranger, ^working for Broadway, television ^d the movies. But it was as a f ^robust, cushy-toned tenor man that he earned his greatest recognition, -and he was never better than when j' going hom-to-hom with Zoot Sims. >>^eir partnership lasted, on-and- off, from the Herman days until - 'Zims' death in 1985. The loss of A1 Cohn's tenor saxophone is a major blow to jazz. He was 62. Delanay I pioneered the jazz discography, ""publishing his Hot Discography in ,.1936. He established the Hot Club of France (from which Django -Reinhardt and Stephane Grappelli took their band name), co-founded Jazz Hot magazine with Hugues Fanassie in 1934 (the magazine still ,f£xists), was director of Vogue Records, wrote a biography of Rein- '«ardt, and was a life-long organizer of jazz events. ' ROLL ON, COLUMBIA, ROLL ON - Those "Columbia Jazz Masterpieces" just keep on coming, J 1 eight new ones have just been i-jcshipped and, as usual, they are an I J odd assortment of reissued albums, I !'"compilations, "best ofs," and what * I jiot. The Quintessential Billie Holiday Volume III continues its march through the CBS sides recorded by the greatest jazz singer them all; 16 tracks covering four glorious months in 1936-37, backed l^y Teddy, Benny, Ben, Pres, guys bice that Louis Armstrong: The Hot 'Fives Volume I is the beginning of what should be a cornerstone in any jazz collection: Louis Armstrong's first sides as a leader. This is it- this is where everything that has taken place in jazz over the past 60 years has its roots. The album contains the first 16 Hot Five sides, recorded in 1925 and 1926, and they hum with brilliance. The orderly, com- plete reissues of all the Armstrong Hot Hves and Hot Sevens is some- thing American jazz fans have been waiting for for years. Woody Her- man: The Thundering Herds 1945-47 is another essential, as well as time- ly, package. Fourteen tracks from the Hrst Herd, two tracks from the Second Herd, and as big a stack of Herman classics as is now available on one record: "Woodchopper's Ball," 'The Goof and I," "Four Brothers," "Blue Rame," "Apple Honey," "Bijou," etc. Duke Ellington's Blues In Orbit is the reis- sue of a 1959 LP plus a couple of extra tracks; solid late-'5()s El- lington. Charles Mingus's Shoes of the Fisherman's Wife is most of the 1959 Mingus Dynasty album, fitted out with some of the solos that had been edited out originally (solos that were restored in a double-LP called Nostalgia in Times Square a couple of years ago), along with, for no apparent reason, "The Shoes of the Fisherman's Wife are Some Jive Ass Slippers," off of I97l's Let My Children Hear Music (why do they do things like that?). Then come two oddball hodge-podge albums: Miles and Coltrane and The Lyrical Stan Getz. The first is bits and pieces of previously-released Miles Davis (Coltrane, you'll recall, was a sideman with Miles, not a co- leader) ft-om '55 and '58 (the first two tracks Miles recorded for Columbia along with the live sides from the Newport Jazz Festival). The second is bits and pieces culled from Stan Getz's Columbia albums - several of the standards and bal- lads off the '70s fusion albums (in- cluding two Chick Corea tunes that became semi-standards) and a 1964 version of "Misty" with Bob Brook- meyer (who comes up with these ideas?). The final album is a sampler. Everything, of course, is digitally remastered and available in every format you can think of. Great stuff, with tons more still to come. ON BLUES - Blues, one of the es- sential bodily fluids of jazz, is also seeing the constant light of reissues. From Delmark comes Roosevelt Sykes' Raining in My Heart, Magic Sam Live, Carey BeU's Blues Harp, Arthur "Big Boy" Crudup's Mood, Robert Jr. Lockwood's Steady Rollin' Man, Sleepy John Estes In Europe, Big Joe Williams's Piney Woods Blues and two anthologies {Sweet Home Chicago and Blues Ptano Orgy). From MCA comes a stack of Chess reissues: Five albums called The Real Folk Blues, one each of '60s material by John Lee Hooker, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Memphis Slim and Sonny Boy Williamson; and Williamson's Down and Out Blues and Buddy Guy's My Blues in San Francisco. EDITORIAL ...So Marshall Was Right L inda Ronstadt continues to break new ground, take chances, and... flourish. I guess we should have realized just what a maverick Ms. Ronstadt was in 1980 when she performed in the Pirates of Penzance on Broadway, on record and in the film. Then there was the dramatic and unexpected What's New concept LP, one of the reigning queens of rock and roll in a forties-style ballroom gown singing forties style ballroom music. Music conducted by the legendary Nelson Riddle, great classics and standards and not a rock and roll note anywhere to be found. She even took the show on the road and played at standing room only audiences of all ages all over the country. The three albums in this series were all certified either gold or platinum. Next was a total departure as Linda teamed up with Emmylou Harris and Dolly Parton for a traditional country album. Trio, also a platinum seller. Now here she comes with an LP of traditional Mexican songs (Canciones de mi Padre), sung totally in Spanish. Not an LP that has an English or Spanish version, if you want this one it's in Spanish only, and it's already gold. Ms. Ronstadt is on the road again with the show for Canciones de mi Padre, not a rock and roll classic in sight... just a mariachi band and Linda. The tour has been sold out from the start. Cash Box spoke to some of the people in attendance at her recent Los Angeles dates and discovered that about 30 percent of them spoke Spanish, the rest didn't understand a word. What we're getting at is Marshall McLuhan. He was right, "the medium is the message." People just want to hear Linda Ronstadt sing, what she sings, how she sings it, doesn't seem to matter. It's nice to see an established superstar take chances and win - yet we are a little leery... when she goes back into the studio the question won't be what's new, it'll be what's next. NEWS Recording Industry Seeking DAT Solution NBS Test Results Women Grab February Gold And Platinum Disappoint RIAA LOS ANGELES - Responding to the results of the Nation^ Bureau of Standards (NBS) study on the copy- code scanner system, Jason S. Ber- man, President of the Recording In- dustry Association of America, Inc. (RIAA), recently pledged to seek a solution to the DAT home taping controversy through "negotiation, legislation or litigation." Although surprised and disap- pointed by the results of the NBS study, Berman commented that RIAA would accept the verdict of the NBS study as it had agreed that it would. Berman emphasized that RIAA was not prepared "to give up the fight on DAT." He said that the major problem of protecting America's music still exists and that "there must be a policy of copyright protection so that music creators can benefit from new technologies instead of being harmed by them." Berman's statement came as a result of findings announced by the NBS test of the copy-code system. The system was proposed by the recording industry as a solution to the inevitable misuse of DAT tech- nology for unlimited taping of CD quality copies of pre-recorded music. According to industry estimates, home taping already results in lost sales of $1.5 billion every year. "We made a good faith effort to find a workable solution to the home taping threat posed by DAT. Working together with the hardware manufacturers we are certain to find an acceptable technological solution. "We will continue to pursue a solu- tion to this problem on any and every front - in the Congress, and in the courts if necessary. Indeed, as I've said in the past, it is our intent to sue any manufacturer that tries to bring DAT machines into the U.S. before this issue is resolved, and we have al- ready established a legal fund for that purpose. NARM '88 Retailers Luncheon Set LOS ANGELES - On the afternoon of March 12, the second day of the 30th annual NARM Convention in Los Angeles, representatives of the NARM Manufacturers Advisory Committee have invited a group of retailers to a working lunch in the Beverly Hills Room of the Century Plaza Hotel. Open to fuU-line record retailers who are not on the NARM Retailers Advisory Committee, this luncheon will provide a valuable opportunity to exchange information and views on current topics of mutual interest with top executives from the six major distribution companies. Pete Jones, Vice President, Dis- tribution of BMG Music and Chair- man of the Manufacturers Advisory Committee, will chair the session. He notes that the agenda will focus on many of the same topics that were discussed at the NARM Retailers Ad- visory Committee meeting in San Francisco last fall. 'This meeting will serve the same purpose as that one (the NARM Retailers Advisory Committee meet- ing)," stated Jones, "...a chance to talk to a small group, not about your own companies concerns, but about the problems and opportunities that are industry-wide." Approximately 40 retail repre- sentatives and 12 manufacture repre- sentatives will be in attendance. Any retailer who has not yet received an invitation should contact the NARM office at (609) 596-2221. Close to 400 people turned to hear Daryl Hall, Ron Del- sener, Allen Grubman, Bob Sum- mers, and Tommy Mottola discuss topics ranging from the history of the music industry in New York, the cur- rent state of the industry, and the state of music today. One concerned a Herb Al- pert show in central park in the 60s when it rained so hard Delsener had to send out to Coney Island for beach umbrellas and have stage hands hold them over the band. "Herb Alpert didn't speak to me for fifteen years after that," Delsener said. NEWS Burns On Radio Vs. Television LOS ANGELES - The gap between the role of radio and the function of television is widening, media guru George A. Burns told broadcast ex- ecutives who attended his 21st Burns Media Radio Studies Seminar in Los Angeles. Burns stated radio has been reduced to a minimal, briefing func- tion in terms of non-musical content, and virtually any listener desire for detail or "in-depthness" is gone. 'The content of our culture has moved to television," Bums stated. 'Trint and radio - particularly radio - are secondary in being the sources of what people know, care and talk about. A growing amount of non- musical content on the radio is about TV. Radio is talked about less and less and has become a utility with as much top-of-mindedness as the water company." These observations, along with other aspects of his state-ot-the- media analysis, were based on con- clusions drawn from the Burns organization's ongoing series of "one-to-one" in-depth interviews conducted nationwide during this year. According to Bums, "People are now picking the morning show be- cause the announcer/disc jockey matches their particular mood that morning, and too much of any con- tent is not a good thing, even humor. In the mornings, music sets the mood. After the mornings, music is the mood. "Listeners now use the radio to choose the mood they want, and they will switch to another station just to change the mood. They usually don't want variety from one station. Eclec- tic radio, which is many moods, is no longer viable in any form." Force M.D/s (Continued from page 8) been scuffing and getting down on our knees on the street, and it's the same way on the stage. Get right down on our knees on that stage, too. Ain't nothing changed. The street is no different from that stage, it's just playing to a bigger audience. You got more technology behind you, and people working for you, and you can make it come out even better. The street is raw. The stage is kind of raw, too." "Our stage show," Trisco chimes in, "is unique. It's just entertaining to a see a rehearsed group with the choreography and the harmonies, get up on stage and present it to you in a workmanship manner, but raw. Instead of seeing another group get up there on just the keyboards, and all this electronic equipment. It takes the fun out of it. You would say to yourself, T can do that.' Right now the Force M.D.'s are lis- tening to demos to select songs for their next record. They're looking forward to being more involved with production this time around and plan to take things in a funky, uptem- po direction. "We're really looking for something different," states T.C.D. "We don't want to sound the same on the radio. We want to be able for you to turn on the radio and say, 'What is THAT?' That's gonna be us. That's the type of sound we're look- ing for." Trisco adds, "When people see us live, they say, 'Wait a minute, they sing that, too?' That's how it is. We try to be diverse about it. We don't want to stick with one particular form be- cause after a while, people get tired of it." 'That's what Force M.D.'s stand for: Musical Diversity," explains Stevie D. "We're very versitile musi- cally. Like T.C. was saying, when you hear a record on the radio you will know it's us. By how veristile our style is. "As long as we're gonna be around, people al- ways gonna be breaking up to make up. So the ballads will definately be there. From the Force M.D.'s." Orders are being taken from distributors, retailers and mail order firms. Paramount Home Video has been engaged in a "Hits Blitz" campaign involving a 10 million dollar ad saturation program. They are at- tempting to increase the "depth of copy^' ratio on their top titles. Says Doctorow, "We've scor^ a resound- ing victory for consumers, since there will be one Beverly Hills Cop II cas- sette for every 100 VCR households in the U.S. The existing average ratio for a hit release is about one to 222." Hence, their debut RCA Records LP, Ruffin & Kendrick marks yet another milestone in the hves of two of rock 'n roll's most legendary per- formers and distinctive vocalists. The Ruffin & Kendrick project in- cludes such niustrious musicians and producers as John Oates, Arthur Baker, Ron Harris, John McFadden and Club Nouveau (who produced a cover of Sly Stone's, It's A Family Affair.) Although iY s been nearly two decades since Ruf- fin and Ken drick shared the spotlight as lead singers of the famous Temptations, the magic of their natural collaboration is more apparent than ever. Eddie's famous tenor continues to soar and scin- tillate, as David's deep, soUd tenor im- erringly provides that raw, basic inim- itable soimd. I As teenagers in Detroit, they sang together in a group called The Primes. Then came their famous association as lead singers of The Temptations, which spurred such songs as My Girl, Get Ready and Ain't Too Proud To Beg. In Ae late '60's, both singers branched out to pTxrsue solo careers. In retrospect, they concur, "we have the same root in common and we can always look back and smile. But we've always looked ahead and e)q?lored new grounds. tM- though they look like the same groimds sometimes, it's a different attitude and a different age. Musically, we are basical- ly interested in love songs, good songs with good lyrics that we picked for this particnilar album." Prior to their recording reunion, Da’vid and Eddie toured Eurof>e and the United States as solo performers "when- ever we felt tike working!" A short time before the Hall and Oates engagement, both had discussed the possib^tiity of working on the road as a team. "And then one night, Kendrick recalls, I was appearing at the Premier Theatre in Detroit and David got up and started singing with me." "From that point on, adds Ruffin, "we've been a team and have toured the coimtry with Mary Wells, Martha Reeves and Mary Wil- son and The Supremes. It's just like the old days except that we're older, wiser and know how to stay out of each other's way! It's really a family affair." Jackson (Continued from page 14) V So there were things missing at the ^^arden. The audience (on this night, ranging from little kids with their moms to Leonard Bernstein) was polite, like they were in a Broadway theatre. They didn't scream, didn't stand and dance, didn't rush the stage. Michael, for all his efforts, never really communicated with the 20,000 in the way that, say, Bruce Springsteen does. He was there, singing and dancing like crazy, but he was something to watch, not the focus of an intense, communal rock 'n' roll experience. And the whole show seemed a lit- tle facile, a little too perfectly-plotted. Not only was 'Thriller" sung, but the video was re-created (complete with wolf mask). Same with "Beat It" and "The Way You Make Me Feel" (similar clothes as in the videos, similar dance steps). Show biz. Broadway. Vegas. What was phenomenal, however, what out-smoked the flashpots and out-shined the lasers was, purely and simply, Michael Jackson singing and dancing. Forget the chotchkas and the special effects, the guy truly is a once- in-a-generation show business talent. "Billie Jean," the best number of the evening - and the best song on either Thriller or Bad - exemplified everything that is wonderful about the man. With a slouch hat over one eye, and a bright, white spotlight directly over his head, Michael Jack- son sang the lyric with an angry, frustrated yelp as he unleashed a jaw-dropping series of dance steps. Gliding, floating, flitting across the stage like magic. He's here, he's there, I-know-I-saw-him-do-it-but-I- don't-believe-he~did-it kind of danc- ing. Unbelievable. In fact, the whole show was a two-hour terpsichorean display the likes of which haven't been since M-G-M folded up its back- lot. Which is, of course, why it took the videos to really put Thriller across. Michael Jackson isn't a singer, he's an entire show business creature. Hearing him is one thing -- if he's got a great song, he's got a great record - but seeing the whole shootin'-match is the only way to ap- preciate the man's talent. Vaudeville is dead, and the idea of Michael Jack- son going on Broadway for a couple of years is absurd. Videos were the answer, and Michael Jackson was canny enough to know that right from the start. But they're nothing compared to seeing him live. Thing is, though, it ain't rock 'n' roll. It's American musical theatre taken to a completely new level. The Michael Jackson Show is an M-G-M all-singing, all-dancing spectacle for the '80s. MAGIC’S RAP AUACK VOLUME III Various Artists (Profile 1249) 75 KISS SERIOUS Chico DeBarge (Motown 6249 ML) 61 23 72 2 68 49 69 63 66 22 65 8 73 21 THE BEAT S UPERBAD JASPER - As an in- tegral member of the Isley Brothers and Isley-Jasper- Isley, Chris Jasper has been at the forefront of progressive R&B miisic since the early 1970's. Now this multi- talented performer is stepping into the spotlight with his premier solo album, Superbad, on CBS Associated Records. Chris Jasper's professional career began in earnest in 1973, when the original Isley Brothers trio expanded to include younger brothers Ernie Isley(guitar) and Marvin Isleyfbass) along with cousin Chris on keyboards. Thenew group made its vinyl debut that same year with the groundbreaking 3+3 album, and followed up with a series of modem rock and roll classics Hke That Lady, Fight The Power, Live It Up and What It Comes Down To. Chris Jasper was a key player, arranger and songwriter on the Isley Brothers' gold and platinum albums like Showdown, Live It Up and 'The Heat Is On. In 1984, Ernie, Marvin and Chris broke away from the Isley Brothers to form Isley-Jasper-Isley. Writing, produc- ing and performing as ecjual partners, the trio released a striking debut LP, Broadway's Closer To Sunset Boulevard. This expert blend of R&B feel and advanceci pop technology yielded two successful singles. Look The Other Way and Kiss And Tell. Isley-Jasper-Isley's second album, Carvan Of Love, appeared in Septem- ber, 1985, with the title track becoming a number one black hit. An acappella ver- sion by the Housemartins later topped the U. K. charts as well. The third Isley- Jasper-Isley LP Different Drummer, was released in April 1987. It included a powerful anti-apartheid anthem called Brother To Brother as well as the roman- tic radio hit Giving You Back The Love. CHRIS JASPER Superbad was written, produced, ar- range and performed by Chris Jasper. The album contains eight tracks, their arrangements built on Jasper's multiple keyboards and carefully layered vcxal harmonies. Givin' AllMy Love is a mid- tempo love song with a syncopated rhythm; Like I Do is a lush baJlad which plays Jasper's intimate lead vocals against his own falsetto background voices. The hard-edged and funky title cut, Superbad, (acheived top 5 chart activity) encouraged kids to stay in school, say no to drugs and look out for each other. The foUow-up single One Time Love has garnered weU over 60 radio station adds in less than three weeks since its release. Look for this to become another major hit for one of the nicest people you will ever meet! A personal favorite of mine. Son Of Man win be serviced to Gospel formats aroimd the country as an album cut The album is appropriately titled, Chris Jasper and his music is S-U-P-E-R-B-A- D!! I ON JAZZ CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS HORTA HEARS A WHO - Brazilian guitarist Toninho Horta (1), who will be releasing his debut Verve Forecast album. G oodman vaults - When Benny Goodman died a couple of years ago, he willed truckloads of materials to Yale University, which established the Benny Good- man Archives. Now Musicmasters, the classical label that has recently begun building up a jazz line (start- ing from the last album Goodman recorded) is set to begin issuing al- bums drawn from the more-than 800 hours of tapes in Goodman's private collection, under an ex- clusive agreement with Yale and the Goodman family. The BGjYale Col- lection, as the series will be called, will debut in May with a smor- gassbord album. Volume I, which will include live and studio small- group and big-band sessions recorded between '55 and '86, 15 tracks in all. "It is an amazing collection, one that will intrigue performers and scholars for generations to come," says Harold E. Samuels, music librarian and professor of music at Yale (and, with Stanley Dance, Morton Gould and Loren Schoen- berg, an annotator of the series). The BG/Yale Collection, Volume I, will be released on Goodman's birthday. May 29. MAX - Max Gordon opened up the Village Vanguard at Seventh Avenue South and lOth Street during Franklin Roosevelt's first term in office and both he (Max) and the club are stiU there. The Van- guard, easily the most famous jazz club in the world, is still the quintes- sential jazz joint: it's smoke-filled, it's dedication is only to music (it's the only club in the city that doesn't sell food and one of the very few that still has three sets a night, seven nights a week), and it still can be something of a bargain (12 bucks is as high as the door charge general- ly goes and, as long as you keep guzzling down drinks and the line up the steep stairs leading to the club isn't too long, they'll let you stay there through all three sets). The other night, in celebration of Max Gordon's 85th birthday, an im- pressive selection of well-wishers jammed into the club (early, mind you. Max wasn't going to give up any of his night's business for some- thing like his own 85th birthday party). Among those pounding Max on the back where Ahmet and Nesuhi Ertegun, Alger Hiss, Syl- via Syms, Illinois Jacquet, Profes- sor Irwin Corey, Bobby Short, Jack Rollins, Orrin Keepnews, Jabbo Smith, and various and sundry other jazz musicians, writers and hangers-on. Max, always glad- hearted at the sight of a packed Van- guard, was beaming. WORDS FROM WYNTON - Wynton Marsalis is a hard guy to figure out. A perennial Grammy winner, he is not reluctant to denounce NARAS (during a New Music Seminar panel discussion two years ago, Wynton said, "Look at the Grammy Awards show. That's just three hours of pure bullshit. And not just bullshit, but pure rascist bullshit."), but he has yet to give back any of his Gram- mys. In any case, he won a jazz Grammy again this year, while he was out of the country, and he felt obliged to draft up an acceptance speech. Here it is: "My tour of Australia prevented me from accepting this Grammy Award in person. This award is particularly special. Receiving eight consecutive Grammy Awards in four years is an affirmation to me, and hopefully a signal to others, that both the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences and my peers have a sincere apprecia- tion for quality in American music and that it is not necessary to use gutter language, sexual innuendos and other trendy gimmicks, designed to exploit the immaturity of adolescents, to be a successful recording artist. It is with great pleasure that I accept this Grammy Award." Charles Weisen- berg is the name of the instructor and $175 is the prices of the fee (ex- cluding the visits to local clubs, where most sessions will take place). I guess things just haven't been going that well for Esther Satterfield. EDITORIAL Metalmania Sweeps Into Yuppieville M ichael Hutchins of INXS interviewed by Jane Pauley on NBC's Today show? Eddie Van Halen, accompanyied by Sammy Hagar, the entire Van Halen band and the all the members of Scorpion, Dokken and Metallica host a full-media press conference, everybody whose anybody shows up and news of a pending nine-hour heavy metal concert makes national news headlines? Something's happening here. Concert promoters confirm that they no longer look to teens to fill up the venue when Rush or Yes or David Lee Roth come to town. Not by a long shot. This audience is now primarilly 25- 40; perhaps because ^e stars are also 25-40 (and above). Heavy metal then, is no longer the music of the rebellous young, making their show one long, loud vulgar gesture against the es- tablishment. Rather it is, ever-increasingly, the music of the es- tablishment. And this establishment enjoys itself. It is a genera- tion not of vipers but of indulgers. Indulgers not in the sense of drugging-out, but of dining out. Indulgers who don't hesitate to cater to their audiophile whims, or to satisfy their fashion preferences. And, somewhere along the line, their musical tastes jumped from Julio Iglesias to Guns and Roses and the record indus^ began to take note. Those of you who still smile when you think of Johnny Mathis crooning "Chances Are," better look for sanctuary. Head for the hills all you lovers of Manhattan Transfer, Creedence Clear- water, and rock the way Elvis rolled it . . . we are at the dawn of new heavy metal day, and it looks like we might have a melt- down.
