THE INDEPENDENT WAY Indie Groove CASH BOX INDIE JAZZALBUMS L abel notes - Rykodisc enters the artist-development arena with the release of Bones and Flowers by Austrailian indie sensations the j Screaming Tribesmen. The ' company is also dipping into the ! video waters with a Tribesmen I video release and “She’s King,” by Marty Willson-Piper, the guitarist of the Church. But wait, there’s more. Coming soon from Ryko are releases from the Residents and Keith Levene, live efforts from Frank Zappa and King Sunny Ade, and yet another installment in the seemingly endless series of “previously unreleased” material by Jimi Hendrix. (This one’s taken from quality BBC recordings circa 1967.) J!Ml HENDRIX, chilling out after a recent club appearance Belated 10th anniversary greet- ings to Sugar Hill Records of Dur- ham, N.C. Sugar Hill is a tireless supporter of roots consciousness, with a roster of artists that reads like a who’s-who of country/folk/ bluegrass music. Over the years Sugar Hill has played host to Ricky ' Skaggs, Leon Redbone, Doc Watson, Jesse Winchester, Jonathan Edwards, David Gris- man and many others. ONE STEP AHEAD OF THE ARM-TWISTERS - One of our favorite press kits in recent months came from a local band called Us, whose single “Layover in London” is available on the Young Raw Records label. The bulk of the material in the press kit is a small review from a national magazine (a magazine that’s famous for its j c iarts, which aren’t nearly as ac- ' curate as ours); this review is presented in a succession of Xeroxed blow-ups, until the final page of the press-kit is a single blurred-out paragraph that swal- lows a whole page. The song, by the way, is a pretty-good Euro- synth-dance number that has been rightly compared to Duran Duran, with epic vocals reminiscent of U2. It’s presented in five different for- mats, three for radio and two for clubs. For a while now the band has been after us for a mention. I’ll be happy to give them a bigger one when they release something more substantial. THEE FOURGIVEN FOUR FOURGIVENS! - One of my favorite garage-fuzz combos. Thee Fourgiven, have added a new member, guitarist Mojo Jones. Their brand of demented power grunge, reminiscent of Alice Cooper, the Cramps and the MC5, is available domestically on the Dionysius label, but it’s in Europe where the band is given its due as mind-blowers. Like fellow psychedelians the Fuzztones, the Blacklight Chameleons and the Miracle Workers (with whom they are playing at White Trash Au-Go- Go in LA. on Aug. 19), they are treated like gurus whenever they cross the ocean, but they are vir- tually unknown over here. What’s wrong with this country, anyway? I’LL TELL YA WHAT’S WRONG WITH THIS COUNTRY ... - While in San Francisco last weekend for the state convention of the Peace and Freedom Party (a socialist sect with big plans for our collective fu- ture), I managed to squeeze in a lit- tle club-hopping and had some of my darker suspicions confirmed about the future of youth culture. Rap is all over the radio (which is okay with me), and at hip hideaways like Nicky’s Bar-B-Que, Nightbreak and Zeitgeist, the dance floors are shaking to outlaw metal, hip-hop, salsa and mutated lounge music, not necessarily in that order. A definite sign of the times was when my hostess, scanning her radio dial for something cool, heard R.E.M. doing "Radio Free Europe” and skipped right past itI Ouch! Keep the faith ... JAZZ ON JAZZ S ALE DAYS - The summer jazz festival season winds down and the musicians return to home base - the jazz clubs of Greenwich Village - to find, egadsl, another jazz festival. The two men above are Mel Litoff (1) and Horst Liepolt and they are the guiding forces behind the Hennes- sy Village Jazz Festival, a festival that is really just a big end-of-the- season jazz club sale. From August 26 - September 5th, a $15 pass (available at the Village Gate and Sweet Basil) gets you into almost every club in the Village for half- price during the first two sets and for free for the third set. That, as any jazz hormd knows, can add up to a large savings, not to mention the fact that the festival kicks-off August 26 with a free Village Gate concert with Ron Carter, Kenny Barron, Bob Berg, Mike Stem, the Dirty Dozen Brass Band, Take 6, and Junior Mance. So it's not really a jazz festival, but it is certainly fes- tival (and it can certainly be a cost- saver) and the line-up in the clubs over that period includes Art Blakey, Abdullah Ibrahim, George Coleman, Alvin Batiste, Illinois Jacquet, John Scofield, Ahmad Jamal, Barry Harris, Dr. John and enough talent worthy of any jazz festival. This whole thing was headed into the toilet before Hen- nessy came up with some sponsor- ship this year, so a toast to the cognac people. START SPREADING THE NEWS “ The New York State New Music Network will send The Max Roach Quartet, the Henry Threadgill Sextett, Philip Glass, the Kronos Quartet, Women of the Calabash and the piano duo Double Edge on a quick tour through the Empire State. The shebang kicks off with a free concert at New York City's Whitney Museum, September 19, featuring I^oach, Glass (who'll be playing solo piano on the tour), and Threadgill, and the groups hit Buffalo's Hallwalls Contemporary Arts Center, Clinton's Hamilton College, Huntington's IMAC/ Inter-Media Art Center and Ithaca's Cornell University during the first two weeks in October. JMT NOTES - JMT, Stefan Winter's forward-thinking West German label - a label that has done more than most to seek out new jazz talent - has signed a licensing agree- ment with PolyGram Jazz. The deal will commence in September with the release of new albums by Cas- sandra Wilson, Hank Roberts, Craig Harris and Bob Stewart. JMT, you'll recall, has been with PolyGram since Winter began the label, but that was an import situa- tion. According to PolyGram, the licensing agreement will allow JMT's prices to drop and will enable the label to increase its recording ac- tivities "three-fold." Upcoming from JMT, albums by Herb Robertson, Paul Motian, Greg Osby (solo and in tandem with Steve Coleman), Robin Eubanks, and Bill Frisell/Jim Hall. BOPPING AROUND - Don't forget the upcoming JazzTimes Convention, set for Los Angeles Oct. 5-8. This year - the first time the Convention is on the West Coast - topics will include "Sunday Jazz Radio," "Where is the Black Jazz Audience," "Ask the Lawyer: Records & Publishing and Per- formers & Presenters." Call (800) 832-2838 for more information. . .New York's Film Forum is schedul- ing a "Jazz on Screen" series to run Oct. 21 -Nov. 10; look for the new (a Belgian documentary on Charlie Parker) and the old (Jazz on a Summer's Day) to be included. . .New York's St. Peter's Church - thanks to Pastor John Garcia Gen- sel, the Shepherd of the Night Flock, the city's jazz ministry - is going to honor Lionel Hampton Oct. 27 with a gala concert and a new award, called the Duke &c The Shepherd Award, to help raise money to extend and continue Gensel's fine work (he's approach- ing retirement); call (212) 935-2200 for information...Rodney Franklin is now signed to RCA's Novus line and his upcoming album for the label. Blues Master Robben Ford By Gene Ferriter Robben Ford is one of the most remarkable guitarists in any idiom, comfortable in a wide range of styles. Most notably he is a blues master with so much finesse that he could single- handedly resurrect popular interest in the genre, much the same way Stevie Ray Vaughan and Robert Cray have done in recent years. His newly released album for Warner Brothers Records is entitled Talk To Your Daughter and was an instant debut on the Cush Box Top Pop Album Chart. Robben has a rich history as a player that includes a tenure with Joni Mitchell, George Harrison, Michael McDonald and the legendary Miles ©Uvis as well as co-founding the Yellowjackets who used to be his back-up band. He has recorded for such diverse acts as Little Feat, Barbara Streisand, Kenny Loggins, Bonnie Raitt and Kiss. Having played in such varied con- tacts, Talk To Your Daughter represents a return to his first real love, the blues."When I listened to the first Paul Butterfield Blues Band album with Mike Bloomfield on guitar, that really started me off playing blues music (ik about age 14). As soon as I heard that record I knew I wanted to be a guitar player." Soon after, Robben was always playing in some sort of band situation, forming the Charles Ford Band with his brother Pat, joining Charlie Musselwhite'sband and later Jimmy Witherspoon in addition to having his own groups. In 1978 Robben released his first solo record for Elektra Records, The Inside Story, which included a supporting cast that would later become the Yellowjackets. In the decade since. Ford has made his mark as une of the most highly regarded sidemen in the business, peaking with his six month stint on tour with Miles Davis (which included the Amnesty In- national concert at the Meadowlands). After parting with Miles, where se was there to go as a sideman? Ford had finally come full circle to his blues roots and decided to make his own record. "I financed a demo along with a partner of mine named Scott Ferguson, ^ho produced the album. We tried to shop a record deal and the first per- son we took it to was Ted Templeman at Warner Brothers. He immediately wanted to sign me, bam, right on the spot.'The performances were so out- L^anding on the demo that Templeman wanted to use the recording un- changed for the album. There are nine songs on the record and six of them are from the original demo. It is very uncommon for a major label to take such an approach, which is an extreme tribute to Ford and the talented players on the album, which includes keyboardist Russell Ferrante, bassist Roscoe Beck, and drummer Vinnie Colaiuta, three of the most in-demand players on their individual instruments. Tipping his hat to blues masters of the past. Talk To Your Daughter contains creative interpretations of classics like Walter Jacob's "Can't Hold Out," Fvooker T.'s"Born Under A Bad Sign"(first recorded by Albert King), B.B. King's"Help The Poor,"Guitar Slim's"! Got Over It,"and of course J.B. Lenoir 's'Talk To Your Daughter."Ford also penned two originals for the ef- P.-rt,"Getaway" and "Can't Let Her Go"and reveals his jazzier dimension through the Russell Ferrante instrumental, "Revelation"and Mose Allison's ' Ain't Got Nothin' But The Blues." Robben's playing smokes throughout tije record and captures the spunk of his live playing like nothing on vinyl. On stage. Ford is one of the most engaging performers on any instrument, i ivariably bringing down the house regardless of the venue or band con- figuration. Those who have seen him live tend to develop an extreme loyal- ty (this reviewer having seen him over twenty times). Recognizing Ford as a true gem, Warner Brothers Records has really rallied behind him, espe- cially for a first time artist on the label. "It's so delightful to see how Warner Brothers is acting" remarks Robben. Talk To Your Daughter finally gives 1 ord's growing base of devout fans a proper dose of his gifted guitar play- i ig and ongoing evolution as a singer, songwriter and arranger. King Diamond By Joe Levy NEW YORK - “People like the feeling of relief after having been scared,” says horror-metal monarch King Diamond. “To be scared, and you're in the middle of something and then you find out, 'Ahh, it wasn't for real' - that's why everybody goes and watches all these horror movies.” Diamond's horror concept albums, Abigail and the new Them (both on Roadracer, the latest distributed through MCA), are fright filled gothic tales set to electric guitar symphonies, with Diamond singing, shrieking, growling, and groan- ing in the voices of different characters in several octaves (sometimes in the same phrase). This is scarifying metal in the tradition of Alice Cooper, Black Sab- bath and, more recently, the likes of Slayer and Mercyful Fate, the Danish metal band Diamond helped found in 1980. And his stage shows are elaborately theatri cal, with a makeup masked Diamond stalking the stage using a microphone stand said to be made of two human bones. “We do something special We try to scare the audience, or at least give them an uneasy atmosphere,” he explains. "Even though we do that they sing along and all that stuff. So I'm sure they're having a great time. And if they didn't, well then, we failed. But it's like, scare them now and then and give them some thrills - that's what we want to put across. 1 know there's not too many bands around doing that. Alice Cooper is one of them, you know, who can really startle people with his stunts. But that's why we try to put that across. Because 1 know that people like the feeling of relief, and knowing that it was only fantasy.” Them is concept album that spins a tale of demonic possession and murder. Diamond defends his subject matter from charges that its violent content can be dangerous or harmful; ”1 don't believe that the heavy metal audience is that stupid that they can't divide between what's real and what's fantasy. If that was really the case, then you should really start forbiding broadcasting news. Be- cause there you get real violence, violence right in your living rooms. And you know that that's for real.” In the underground world of heavy metal, where there is no radio play, not much (if any) record company promo support. King Diamond's sales statistics are very impressive. It's a familiar story of hard working musicians, devoted fans, and steady sales, similar to Megadeath's and Metallica's major label deals and the recent Noise Records/CBS distribution pact. Abigal so\d more than 125,000 copies, and with distribution from MCA and a 55 city tour already underway. Them should do even better. As for Diamond himself, despite his recent move from his native Denmark to L.A. he says he's a stay at home kind of guy. ”1 don't go out that much. 1 prefer staying home and watching horror movies and listening to CDs." He lists The Shining, The Amityville Horror and The Hunger among his favorite horror flims. ”1 rather like the occult stuff, because that gives me the creeps. I know that could be real. When they show a devil with horns in the forehead and all that, I know that's not for real. All these powers that lurk in the backround and suddenly they appear and do things, I can relate to that.” C ash Box September 3, 1988 11

ON JAZZ CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS BIG BOSS MAN— Faster than you can say Bird, George Benson has been signed to play Wes Montgomery in an upcoming film called The Boss Guitar. Right guy, seems to us. L ove for sail - You say you've had enough of jazz festivals? That if you hear about one more jazz festival you'll jump into the river and drown? Well, here's a festival where that can be made easy for you, although it's the Caribbean you'll be drowning in. If it's Oc- tober (or if it's going to be October real soon) it's time for NCL's sixth annual Floating Jazz Festivals. That's right, a jazz festival at sea - in fact two jazz festivals at sea, on the Norway, the world's largest cruise ship, from October 22-28 and the new M.S. Seaward the following week. As the ships cruise the Carib- bean, you can cruise the on-board jazz clubs - listening to the likes of Dizzy Gillespie, Illinois Jacquet, Marion Williams, Benny Carter, Red Rodney and Clark Terry (on the Norway), Joe Williams, Lionel Hampton, Scott Hamilton, Al Grey and Dave McKenna (on the Seaward), and Milt Hinton, Flip Phillips, Buddy Tate, Mel Powell, and Gus Johnson (on both). It's a little bit of paradise right here on earth, as musicians think up every seafaring tune they know (plenty of "My Ship" and "How Deep is the Ocean" on these things), the sun shines bright on ship and ports (in- cluding Ocho Rios, St. Thomas, St. John, and Grand Cayman), and everybody hangs out with a nice healthy glow and a wide smile. If you've got the time, the money, and the inclination, it's a pretty good way to hear some mainstream jazz. Call your travel agent, as they say, or (800) 327-7030. IN THE SAME GENERAL AREA - Miami, that is. Where the Floating Jazz Festivals depart from and where, from December 2-11, New Music America will settle in for a hell of a festival. To go into the details here would take up too much room. Suffice it to say that the participants in this new music blowout will include Ornette Coleman & Prime Time, Ornette Coleman/Pat Metheny, James Blood Ulmer, Jamaaladeen Tacuma, Terrence Simien and the Mallet Playboys, George Adams/Don Pullen, Bill Frisell, Steve Lacy/Irene Aebi/Frederic Rzweski, Anthony Davis, Michele Rosewoman, Marilyn Crispell, Roscoe Mitchell, Astor Piazzolla, the Kronos String Quartet, Nana Vasconcelos and many, many, many others. Interested? It does sound interesting, doesn't it. (305) 347-3768's their number. A BIT WESTWARD - Yes, there's a dry-land jazz festival com- ing up for you landlubbers, and it doesn't get much drier than Sedona, Arizona, which calls its fete Jazz on the Rocks. On September 24, Obo Addy, James Morrison/Adam Mako wicz, Diane Schuur with The Count Basie Orchestra and Richie Cole will be blowing up a storm in that healthy setting (we're talking about an outdoor amphitheatre with red standstone spires). Call (602) 282-1985 if you'd like to high- tail it out there. WHILE WE'RE ON THE SUB- JECT OF THE FUTURE - New York's Town Hall, one of the city's very best concert halls, wants to be in your face this season, so they've concocted an interesting selection of events to draw attention to them- selves and customers to their seats. Included is a series called the Not Just Jazz Festival, and while it's not a festival (it's a series, like I said), it is well-titled. It ain't just presenting jazz, nosireebob. The whole megil- lah goes like this: The Art Ensemble of Chicago (10/29), Allen Tous- saint/Moses Rascoe (11/12), Meredith Monk/Nurit Tilies (12/10), John Zorn with Wayne Horvitz, Bobby Previte, Fred Frith and Bill Frisell (2/25/'89), Abbey Lincoln/Geri Allen/Cassandra Wilson/Steve Coleman (3/4), The World Saxophone Quartet (3/18), and Oregon (4/15). BOPPING AROUND - Glen- dale, CA's Advanced Music Com- pany and Night Life Records have acquired the Sea Breeze Record Company from John Brechler... Verve has just released, as they said they would, two of Betty Carter's excellent self-produced Bet-Car al- bums: The Betty Carter Album and The Audience with Betty Carter, a double album (both available on CD for the first time). Also just reis- sued from those same folks are a pair of Errol Garner's Emarcy al- bums: The Original Misty (it used to be called Contrasts but, yes, it does have Garner's first recording of "Misty" on it) and Mambo Moves Gamer, each with a pair of extra tracks. ..The American Federation of Jazz Socities provides an interesting service, a national Block Booking Assistance Program, giving the lit- tle guys the opportunity to bring the big acts into town with a minimum of travel expense (if they're in the area, how much could it be?). If this is relevant to you, call the AFJS at (912) 927-4438. Solid stuff most of the way (on two-LPs or one-CD). A TRIBUTE TO JOHN COLTRANE: BLUES FOR COLTRANE - Impulse 42122 - Producers: Bob Thiele, Ken Glancy A stick-to-the-ribs modal blowing date by a coterie of Coltrane associates - McCoy Tyner, Pharoah Sanders, Cecil McBee and Roy Haynes - with David Murray tossed in for good measure on three tunes (two on the LP). The spirit here is very strong indeed. THE HOOPS McCANN BAND PLAYS THE MUSIC OF STEELY DAN - MCA 42202 - Producers: Joe Roccisano It's a natural - many of the session guys who infused Steely Dan with jazzy steel are together and blowing on this well-arranged (by Joe Roccisano main- ly) date. Steely fans and West Coast big band fans'll eat this up. MARIANO ~ Charlie Mariano - Intui- tion 90787 (dist: Capitol) ~ Producers; Mike Herting, Paul Shigihara The expatriate reedman blows in from West Germany on this new age-y (Mariano was an early experimentgr with east-west fusions), but quite tasiy, date; a trio Tvith guitarist Paul Shigihara and keyboardist Mike Herting. CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS ON JAZZ BIRD-YHARRY- That's Clint Eastivood (r) directing Forest Wiitaker (1) as Charlie Parker and Sam Wright as Dizzy Gillespie in the eagerly-awaited Bird, coming to the large screen on September 30th.M ore master- pieces - When Columbia started its Jazz Masterpieces series I - jazz skeptic that I am - figured, "This'll start out big and, in two or three releases, fizzle to an in- audible hum." I was wrong. The releases just keep barrelling out; there's no stopping them. I am not complaining, I am delighted. Columbia, which claims to be sell- ing these like hotcakes, is also delighted. In any case, the latest batch goes something like this: Thelonious Monk: The Composer (with liner notes written by yours truly - not bragging, just getting those conflict-of-interest questions out of the way), featuring an un- released "Blue Monk" and 10 tracks pulled from Monk's Columbia records, spotlighting, in different settings, 11 of the man's greatest compositions; The Essential Count Basie Volume 3, swinging, pre-War brilliance; Miles Davis In Person At The Blackhawk Volume 1, the '61 album that features Wynton Kelly on tenor; Jam Sessions From the Vault, alternate takes (and one previously- unreleased track) from the '53 and '56 Buck Clayton-led jam sessions (jammers include Coleman Haw- kins, Freddie Green, Buddy Tate, Joe Newman, Milt Hinton, Jo Jones, Ruby Braff, Billy Butter- field and Clayton) that came out originally as All the Cats Join In; Slipped Disc, 17 '45 and '46 sides from, mainly, the Benny Goodman Sextet of the period (including Red Norvo and Teddy Wilson); Louis Armstrong: The Hot Fives & Hot Sevens, absolutely, positively, without any question, indispen- sible; The Quintessential Billie Holiday Volume 4, the march of the complete Billie Holiday continues unabated and these 1937 tracks are absolutely, positively, without any question, indispensible; and a sampler. SONY, THANK YOU FOR THE SUNSHINE YOU BRING It seems to me that since Sony took over CBS Records, we've been get- ting a lot of Japanese fusion acts released domestically. Seem that way to you? Well, in case it doesn't, the Bottom Line will be the site, from September 20-25, of "East Meets West," a six-night extravan- ganza of - you guessed it - CBS's jazz acts from both sides of the Pacific. Sony is going to shoot the whole thing in high definition video and Japan's NHK TV network will broadcast it. The line-up goes like this: Full Circle/Donald Harrison & Terence Blanchard (9/20), Kimiko Itoh/Kirk Whalum (9/21), Eddie Gomez/The Gadd Gang (9/22), Brian Slawson/Steve Smith and Vital Information (9/23), Osamu/Harry Connick Jr./Bran- ford Marsalis (9/25), Nancy Wil- son/Masahiko Satoh (9/25). ENJOY THE GELT - The Meet The Composer/Reader's Digest Commissioning Program, a new music program fund^ by $750,000 from the Reader's Digest and $200,000 from the National Endow- ment of the Arts, has named its first recipients. Jazzwise they are Max Roach (winner of a recent $372,000 MacArthur Fellowship), $22,500 for a project with the Berkeley and San Diego Repertory Theatres; Ornette Coleman, Henry Threadgill and Alvin Curran, $1 7,000 for pieces for the Rova Saxophone Quartet; and The String Trio of New York, $12,000 for themselves. BOPPING AROUND - Sea Breeze Records is about to release three DAT's: Tom Talbert's Things As They Are, Introducing Roger Neumann's Rather Large Band, and Rob McConnell & The Boss Brass's Live in Digital. ..MTV get ready: Columbia is releasing a video for "Lester Leaps In" from the Bird soundtrack. Sezthe band: (“Tiffany can kiss our [backsides].” MORE GOOD NEWS FOR ANGRY YOUNG TODDLERS Ah cazar Records, in the tiny media mecca of Waterbury, Vt., has just started a children’s label, Alcazam, whose debut offering is Stardc&amer, by Priscilla Hardman. Bertil Angell, genera! manager of the company, said the hew label is for parents "who are looking for quality entertainment ’ and socially responsible music for their kids.” Hear, hear! < Alcazar has also announced the upcoming release of Odetta: Christmas Spirituals, a holiday sampler from folk chanteuse Odet- ta. Alcazar’s latest offering is Tie One On, the new release from folk virtuosos Different Shoes. Dif- ferent Shoes go for that backwoods sincerity sound that’s all the rage i these days. They’ve got the requisi- te acoustic instrumentation, and their materia! ranges from Celtic ^Iftunes to Delta blues to hillbilly jigs to heartbroken balladry, all woven ’ together by a sense of the land and the gentle rhythms of rural life. It’s ^easy to forget that there are still corners of this country where a dul- cimer, a fiddle and a plaintive voice speak louder than a mountain of amplifiers. BUT HEY, YOU DON’T HAVE TO BE A SENSITIVE LUMBER- JACK OR AN ANGRY PRE- TEENAGER TO MAKE QUALITY MUSIC - Lloyd Price, whose long- ago hits include “Personality,” "Stagger Lee,” and “Lawdy Miss Clawdy,” has returned to the record industry as president of NFS, a New Yok-based indie record label who will release the debut album from his new group, the LPO Band, in September ... And, I have in my hand at this very moment the new album from Dorian Harewood, the actor. I’LL BE RIGHT THERE!” OOPS! - We received the press release, but somehow we forgot to pass along the good news about the Chariton Heston Celebrity In- vitational, which was a pistol- shooting competition for gun-totin’ celebs, held Aug. 26-29 at a fancy resort near San Diego. The com- petition was a fundraiser for the In- stitute for Legislative Action, the political arm of the National Rifle Association. (They’re the folks that do such a good job of blocking gun- control legislation every time it comes before Congress.) The list of patriotic participants in the star- studded event ranged from male role-models Arnold Schwar- zenegger and Herve Villechaize to the actress who played Eilie Mae Clampett, the actor who played Sheriff Lobo, the guy who sang the Love Boat theme, and the Beav himself, Jerry Mathers. (If the thought of the Beaver wield- ing a gun makes you a little queasy, you’re missing the point. And so are we. Cash Box is a music magazine. The only press-release propagan- da we know what to do with is music industry propaganda.) Keep the faith ... JAZZ v ON JAZZ S NAP JUDGEMENTS Milt Hinton is one of jazz's great bassists, no two.ways about it. A 78-year-old veteran of the big bands, recording studios, and more pick-up dates than you can count, Hinton is high- ly-regarded, far and wide, for his big tone, his sturdy accompani- ment, his tasty solos, and his mastery of such dying forms as good-old slap bass. But what few people knew until several years ago is that Milt Hinton has, for more than 50 years, been quietly shooting photos of his daily activities, been steadily document- ing one man's journey through 50 years of American music. Finally, after a good deal of planning. Temple University Press has just published Bass Line: The Stories and Photographs of Milt Hinton by Hin- ton and collaborator David G. Berger ($39.95). It is an extraordi- nary book - a beautifully-bound tome that is both a straight-forward autobiography and, more impor- tantly, an album of some 200 wonderful photographs. Hinton shoots photos as a hobby and he is no Richard Avedon or Ansel Adams. But he has captured glimpses of his fellow musicians, and the jazz life in general, that few photographers have ever had ac- cess to. The reason is simple: Milt Hinton was on the inside, and the faces that stare out from these pages are faces filled with honesty; not faces posing for a photographer, faces looking at a friend, a fellow traveller on that difficult jazz road. Some of the images are spectacular, and they are greatly enchanced by the plain-spoken autobiography, which so eloquently and modestly puts the pictures in focus - frames them, as it were. The above image, of Cab Cal- loway, Hinton's longtime employer, and some kids in Florida 50 years ago is just one example. Some of the book's highlights in- clude an achingly moving photo of Billie Holiday at one of her final recording sessions, listening to a playback with tears in her eyes; Ben Webster, with a look in his eyes that explains why they called him "Brute," standing at a New York bar; a picture of a frighteningly young Dizzy Gillespie asleep on a train; a photo of a pained Lester Young at the end of his life; such im- ages as Tyree Glenn and Chu Berry in North Carolina in 1940 in front of a sign that reads "Hamburgers, Hot Dogs, Lunches For Colored Only" and Shad Collins, Mario Bauza, Doc Cheatham, Ike Quebec and Mona Hinton standing and point- ing up at an Alabama establishment that, in 1949, was apparently called "Motel For Colored"; Eubie Blake and Willie "The Lion" Smith, look- ing like two old card sharps, back- stage at the Newport Jazz Festival; Cozy Cole, looking dapper and sinister, standing on a Harlem street in 1939 flanked by two gorgeous young ladies; a very young, very hip Phil Woods at a '57 record date; Louis Armstrong in a Seattle hotel room surrounded by recording devices, and behind-the-scenes photos from two of the most famous all-star gatherings of jazz musicians ever: the Esquire photo shoot that gathered many jazz greats on a Har- lem stoop, and the CBS telecast. The Sound of Jazz, the most famous jazz television show ever. Jimmy Rushing, Count Basie, Thelonious Monk, Charles Min- gus, Sam Cooke, Sarah Vaughan, Benny Goodman, Aretha Franklin, Alec Wilder, Earl Hines, Johnny Hodges, all here in ways that you've rarely seen them: at work, at rest, at ease. Like I said, the photo angles aren't always the best, the lighting isn't always perfect, but the images are lasting, the view into the world of a single veteran jazz par- ticipant and observer - Milt Hinton - is delightful and eye-opening. And the stories about a long, op- timistic life on the road are refresh- ing and insightful. Bass Line is an important work. While we're on the subject of books. Da Capo Press keeps up its steadfast jazz series with two volumes: the first American print- ing of The Essential Jazz Records Volume One: Ragtime to Swing by English critics Max Harrison, Char- les Fox and Eric Thacker (SI 4.95, paperback), an opinionated, worthwhile and very English look at the records of the pre-Bebop Eras, and a paperback reprint of Richard Hadlock's clear-headed 1965 Jazz Masters of the 20s (SI 0.95) with a new introduction and index. COAST TO COAST GOOD VIBRATIONS - Brian Wilson greets A&M recording artist Toni Childs following her recent sold-out showcase at the Roxy Theatre. Other notable fans who turned out at Childs' performance included Julian Lennon, Terri Nunn (of Berlin fame) and Mariel Pastor. L ive & hard - Last Tuesday (9/13), Coca-Cola and the Hard Rock Cafe hosted "Coca-Cola Presents: Live, The Hard Rock," a one-hour live television special that aired on the NBC television network and benefited the homeless of America. Dan Aykroyd hosted the Lome Michaels-produced event, which com- bined comedy sketches with live musi- cal entertainment. The special was broadcast before an outdoor audience in Sparticus Square on the backlot of Universal Studios here in Los Angeles. A BENEFIT FOR THE HOMELESS Comedy was provided by Aykroyd, John Candy, Lorraine Newman, Chevy Chase and Jon Lovitz. Live- musical interludes came from INXS, Toni Childs, The Blues Brothers with Sam Moore, Ziggy Marley & The Melody Makers, and a joint f>erfor- mance courtesy of Paul Simon and John Cougar Mellencamp (who per- formed together for the first time ever). All proceeds from specialized t-shirt sales (available both at the show and through mail order) will be donated to the homeless through the Hard Rock Cafe Foimdation. DRIVE ALL NIGHT - Drive All Night, an innovative 12-piece R&B band, have been generating quite a bit of noise around town lately with their specialized brand of nouveau rhythm and soul. The band - comprised of six horns, four rhythm players and two singers (a highlight is the masterful guitar playing of Adam Levy) - inter- sperses original tunes with a select number of well-chosen and re-ar- ranged covers. You can catch the band performing at At My Place's seventh anniversary celebration on October 10. ADDICTED TO IGGY - Fresh on the heels of the release of their major label debut LP (Nothing's Shocking, Warner Bros.), local boys done good Jane's Addiction, have linked up with the incomparable Iggy Pop for a two- week tour in the nation's capitol. "THE WAVE" IS SWELLING - Los Angeles' KTWV-FM ("The Wave") have announced plans to introduce live announcers to identify music programmed on the station. In addi- tion, the station has added over 500 new cuts to its playlist. The decision to expand the playlist and add DJ's (in the past the station had no on-air personalities) was an- nounced by KTWV Vice President and General Manager Allan D. Cholwitz. "The changes are in direct response to our listeners and to research which con- firmed that the highest level of frustra- tion for our audience was the lack of music identification," Cholwitz stated. "The annovmcers will identify the music in a very brief, low-key manner. The overpowering DJ personalities of other formats, which many adult lis- teners find objectionable, will never be part of The Wave." Announcers are expected to be on the air within two weeks. DANCE FEVER - Capitol Records has announced the launch of a new 12" dance label, designed to accommodate the label's increasing number of dance- oriented releases. A special label and jacket have been created to identify a record as a dance label release. Initial releases will come from S-Express, Suave and The Boogie Boys. Future releases will include Johnny Clegg & Savuka, Mazelle, Cheyanne, M.C. Hammer and others. Until next week... Tom De Savia Los Angeles D reams are free, but BOOKS COST MONEY - Look, I'm sorry to admit it, but I read that Albert Goldman bio of John Lennon last week (The Lives Of John Lennon, WU- ham Morrow & Company, $22,95) and at this very moment iti s stiU burrowing around my insides making me sick, sorta tike I swallowed a live rodent. It's my own fault. I knew the book was a fuzzy little piece of squirming vermin flesh when the freebie review copy ar- rived, but figuring it wouldn't be right to hate it without giving it a chance, I opened to a random page and read. Neat. Just like TV. You can start anywhere (you know the plot by now), time in for as long as you tike, and quit whenever you want. And for a while was interesting enough. I got a couple of good reasons for hating the book (as a pyscho-bio it's a jumble of pathetic baby talk Freud, as a history it's a junior high school social studies project: tell everything you know, leave out everything you don't and pretend it doesn't exist). Only then I couldn't stop reading it, even when the narrative's ceaseless and meaning- less flow of self-degradation, personal violence, and bad sex (again, just tike TV) was making me feel sick. It was worse than junk food, worse than junk culture. It was pure junk, tike the junk Goldman reveals John and Yoko spiked into their veins upon occassion. Ab- solute mind numbing garbage. John and Yoko hated each other. John hated his body. John hated Paul. Yoko was manipulative. If you didn't know these things, if you couldn't guess these things, Goldman spells them out in convincing detail. But do you care about this stuff? There's a gulf between the emotional content of Lennon's music and the book's sorrid biographical revelations that Goldman never even attempts to bridge. Which leaves me wondering just what the point of the whole thing is anyway. (And I would't dare suggest it was writ- ten to make money. Gee, that'd be cyni- cal.) There's no light, no love, no pas- sion, no contrast here to make the shmy underbelly of Lennon's life seem the "S least bit important. Gripes, these days the entertainment industry puts performers under mind destroying pressure and then bitches when their minds are destroyed by drugs, drink, or thirty cups of coffee a day (the latter being one of Lennon's many habits). And in today's dimate a The Lives Of John Lennon fits right in with the Just Say No hysteria. Not an ^ once of compassion. No real attempt to ^ understand why popular culture eats its young. Just a freak show. Bleeech. , REASONS TO NOT WORRY (BE HAPPY) - After that rant, here's a,- couple of bits of good news: the new Feelies record on A&M, only life, is' • about as great as everyone thought The\. _ Good Earth was. ..National Public Radio is airing a 52 week (!) series called Afropop focusing on the wide variety of African popular music. I rWliles Davis: Sketches Of A Trumpeter By Lee Jeske p.| ^ NEW YORK - Miles Davis sits shirtless in his Hqw York hotel suite - a suite he’s occupied ^since he and his wife Cicely Tyson separated - ; arra contemplates things. big fat airline attendant told me... I said, " 'Who’s that pretty girl over there?’ He said, ‘That’s my back-up.’ Hahahaha. You always haye to have a back-up.” Musically, Miles Davis is the king of the back- U[i7s, the master at pulling new musical rabbits of his hat. Bebop. Poof! ‘‘Birth of the Cool.” Sh^azam! Modalities. Ta-dah! Fusion. Voila! ' And on and on. On this particular day in New l' ^^rk, the man is bitching; he’s not happy about the way his band is going. He’s getting itchy, you Can feel it, he seems to be thinking about digging .i«to the hat for another rabbit. jWhen Miles Davis was coming up -the brash, well-bred mid-Westerner shadowing Charlier ^;^'ker around New York some 40 years ago - things were different. I “In the first place, there weren’t enough ^ "iGCords out there for me to copy,” he says. * '^here was no copying then. Like, now, ' everybody who can play a whole chord has a 1 recording. What are you going to say after that? When I was coming up, I was just hating to be '' "Compared to other trumpet players, you know, •; b-gcause I didn’t get in music forthat. I was trying play like Dizzy at the time, but I couldn’t. I told 'Leonard Feather, ‘I wish I could play like Dizzy.’ 'Ij ** “Dizzy and I talked and I said, ‘Why can’t I play y Jjke you?’ He said, ‘You do. You play the same style, you play the same chords, but it’s just in a i lower register.’ ” .Miles Davis has been quoted as saying the j thing he’ll be remembered for is his sound. That sensuous, slow, vibratoless trumpet sound is, no J ^^_atter what context it’s been placed in over the i decades, one of the most distinctive, and most instated, sounds in American music. “1 developed that sound when I was 13,” he i says. “That’s a mid-Western sound. I’ll tell you who else had that sound. Bunk Johnson. I used ^4\^go around with him - he could hardly move around when he first came to New York, and he ccJuld only play in E-flat. l«'^^‘‘But that sound is the way you play in St. I Louis, trumpet players. Clark Terry has that I sound. The raw sound in St. Louis is like the way I ” f play. My teacher played like that, Elwood Buchanan, I used to love to hear him play. I ‘ And there was this guy named Levi, he had f 'iTic tone. He was crazy. All the trumpet players [ t^sed to say, ‘Levi’s getting out of the rest house [ oday, let’s go to his house and listen to his tone.’ But he went off, like he would start laughing and couldn’t stop.” That sound, when brought East, didn’t always meet with the greatest response. "I used to get made fun of by white players when I played,” says Miles, “’cause I didn’t play like they did. I remember once, Gunther Schuller was with the Metropolitan Opera Band, and they came to Toronto when I was playing there. This is in ’48. He said, ‘You want to try?’ So I sat down with them. One of the trumpet players said, 'Play “Body and Soul.” ’ So I started, and I played it, but they were making fun of my tone. Because they play a legitimate way, you know. And that means the whole world should be wearing the same suit. “So I told Gunther, I said, 'Man, it doesn’t bother me, because there’ll come a time when all of them will have to play like this in order to play in a pop band.’ Which is now. Now if you don’t have that sound that I have, or close to it, they don’t want you to play lead or nothing.” That sound will next be heard on album, ironi- cally enough, back on Columbia Records, which Miles left a few years ago for the greener finan- cial pastures of Warner Bros. He hasn’t jumped labels, but Columbia’s been sitting for several years on a suite that Danish trumpeter Palle Mik- kelborg wrote for Miles several years ago, a suite that was recorded in Denmark with the Danish Radio Orchestra before Miles left Columbia. Then, he says, he’s contemplating a live album from his recently completed world tour. The current band, which Miles is expressing dissatisfaction with, is, like all of Miles’ bands for some 20 years, a fusion band. About the birth of fusion music. Miles shrugs: “Joe Zawinul and I, everytime we’d meet, we’d discuss trying to get Cannonball Adderley to play a little outside of the chords. And Joe had that Rhodes piano, and they used to double the bass line with the bass, which sounded really good. And Cannonball was a funky player anyway, you know, that’s just his background. So, anyway, I got together with Paul Buckmaster and said, 'Paul, write me a bass line like James Brown.’ That was for 'Bitches Brew.’ And Joe was al- ready writing like that, everybody was going that way anyway. All atonce, everybodyjustturned.” Miles Davis, who has been slowly working on his memoirs with writer Quincy Troupe, has a long memory. And his memory seems par- ticularly strong when he’s remembering injus- tices that have been done to him during his career. I ask him about Bird, the Charlie Parker screen biography, which he hasn’t seen yet. “There are different sides of Bird. I never was that close to him, because me and him used to get into things, you know. He’d say, ‘What are you smiling about?’ I’d say, ‘It’s just a natural thing in my face.’ Shit like that. “The things he did I didn’t like. Like catering to white people. He would come on stage and we’d have, say, 30 seconds to end a song before intermission. He would come on stage and say, ‘Bap!,’ and cut it off. And all the white people would laugh. And to me that wasn’t funny. “I remember once Milton Berle came down to the Three Deuces and he made fun of our band. He’s sitting at a table and he said to this group he was with, ‘They’re headhunters.’ I always remembered that. “So I saw him once when I was in first class on a plane - now this was about 20 years later or maybe longer. And I said, ‘Milton, my name’s Miles Davis, I’m a musician.’ He said, ‘Yeah, I know.’ I said, ‘You did something to us years ago that I’ve always remembered and I always said if I ever get close enough to breathe on you that I was going to tell you the way I felt.’ It was so long ago, but I was getting that anger again. “I said, ‘You know, I didn’t like that. And none of the band liked it, those who heard it.’ “And he said, Tm very sorry.’ “I said, ‘I know you are. You are now.’ “And I went back and sat down.” C ish Box September 24, 1 988 11

A s OAGY ON THEIR MINDS Hoagy Carmichael was le of America's greatest ^ songwriters; a brilliant ‘tunesmith whose melodies beautifully balanced the zesty spirit of 20th Century America with the slow, rolling tempo of i/fl9*th Century America, specifically the measured rhythms of the American lAid-West and South. His music, unlike 2^j.|jat of any of his contemporaries, i drawls; it's unhurried, uncomplicated best of all, impretentious American ret’sic, informed by the sounds of jazz, blues and early country music. ..The Indiana Historical Society, in Company with the Smithsonian Collec- tion of Recordings, has just released Hoagy Carmichael's Biograph or 5 Crossroads - a four-LP, three-cassette, 57- tjack compilation of the music of Hoagy 'Carmichael (who, when he wasn't writ- his own lyrics, was blessed with such lyricists as Mitchell Parish and Johnny Mercer): The Classic Hoagy Car- michael. It is a classic, and classy, pack- ' 'j ^ agp, containing a beautiful and higly-in- formative 64-page book by the album's producer John Edward Hasse. ^ ^The producers have gone out of their way to find brilliance; to find perfor- mances that put the music in the very J;:est light. They are not shy about in- cluding several versions of important i'ongs: "Stardust," for example, that standard of standards, is done here by .4£*rmichael himself, Louis Armstrong, Frank Sinatra, Artie Shaw and his Or- clTestra, Ella Fitzgerald and Wynton ( .-Marsalis. Carmichael's own charming, laid-back vocals are peppered throughout this set as are such other first-rate Carmichael interpreters as Bix ^Beiderbecke, Maxine Sullivan, Ethel Waters, Mel Torme, Ray Charles ("Georgia on My Mind," of course), Crosby, the Mills Brothers, Mildred Bailey, Billie Holiday and 5enny Goodman. The songs? Well, you know many of the songs - "How Little We Know," "Rockin' Chair," "Small Fry," "Two Sleepy People," "Skylark, "The Nearness of You," "Heart and Soul," "Lazy River," "I Get Along Without Your Very Well," "New Orleans," and "Old Buttermilk Sky" - but many of them are lesser-known - like "Bread and Gravy" and "Moonbum" - though no less charm- ing, witty and graceful. The Classic Hoagy Carmichael is avail- able at the Smithsonian or from the In- diana Historical Society, 315 W. Ohio St., IndianapoUs, IN 46202 (317-232-1882) for $42 postpaid. PASSING ON - Lawrence Brown, the trombonist whose distinctive, creamy sound graced the Duke El- lington Orchestra from 1932-51 and again throughout the '60s, died Septem- ber 5th in Los Angeles at the age of 81. Lawrence Brown, the last member of the classic Ellington bands of the '30s, had been inactive for most of the past 20 years. Charlie Palmieri, the roaring, hell- bent salsa pianist, and brother of bandleader Eddie Palmieri, died of a heart attack September 12 in the Bronx. Palmieri, who was two-parts salsa, one- part jazz, and all parts rhythmic heat, was 60. And James Black, the New Orleans- based jazz drummer, died August 30 in New Orleans at the age of 48. ROLL ON - Biograph, that historical- minded little Chatham, New York label, has just come out with a new set of his- torical-minded CDs, three of them taken from old piano rolls - James P. Johnson; Carolina Shout, George Gershwin: Rhap- sody in Blue, Fats Waller Classic Jazz Solos From Rare Piano Rolls - and Three Shades of Blues, with recordings by Bukka White, Skip James and Blind Willie McTell. It's particularly fascinat- ing hearing Waller, Gershwin (although the Gershwin disk features only a few roUs originally cut by Gershwin) and Johnson in digital sound. Some of the nuances might be lost, but those piano rolls are crisp, clear and, in a way, scary; it's as if old Fats or James P. were tickling the ivories right there in your living room. CALL FOR... - Philip Morris, no? Yes. The cigarette gigimdamo is spon- soring a whale of a jazz tour, one that will sneak in a quick U.S. date (New York's Town Hall, October 7) before heading on a five-week tour of Europe and Asia (where Philip Morris sells some cigarettes, believe you me). It's an impressive three-band line-up. Band one: James Moody, Curtis Fuller, Diane Schuur, Hank Jones, Billy Higgins, Dave Holland. Band two: Johnny Grif- fin, Bobby Hutcherson, Kirk Lightsey, George Mraz, Kenny Washington. Band three: the Ahmad Jamal Quartet Sounds good, no? The New York quickie is a benefit for WBGO-FM. BLACK CONTEMPORARY THE MET CENTER, MIN- NEAPOLIS, MN - The Met Center in Minneapolis played host to the stateside debut of Prince's Lovesexy tour Wednesday night. Sept. 14. From the time the lights went out until the last note was played, the crowd of 13,000, which included numerous record, radio and musical guests, was taken on an unforget- table trip to the farthest reaches of Utopia. Prince made his entrance by cir- cling the 5,600 square foot, tri- leveled, theatcr-in-the-round stage in a white 1967 Thundcrbird. This is no ordinary stage: It is outfitted with hydraulic lifts, windmakers, a swing set, a basketball hoop, neon sign.s, trapdoors and a bod. The stage is designed so that there is not a bad seat in the house. It sits in the center of the arena with runways and plat- forms facing every section of the audience. JAZZ ON JAZZ IRD - Finally, after years and years of stops and starts, the Charlie Parker story has hit the silver reen. Clint Eastwood, of all pie, is the guy who made it hap- pen and his two-hour-and-forty- Aminute epic will open in New York on Friday (Sept. 30) after two New ''-^rk Film Festival screenings at the j^ginning of the week. You want to like this movie. It . hl^eds with earnestness, it's loaded I with concern and care and intel- V ligence, it tries - it tries really, really hard. And it's got an incredible per- formance by Forest Whitaker (above) in the title role. Unforun- tafely. Bird, for the most part, is a muddle. A nearly three-hour mud- ' »^dle. The film gives us Charlie Parker in the last few years of his troubled ^hfe, skipping back every so often to significant earlier moments. The i^mous Kansas City cutting session, ^where a young Charlie Parker was ^ fiidely chased from the stage when jd Jones sent a cymbal crashing f near his feet, is used and reused, for ^example. Bird gives us Parker, basi- ^ cally, from the eyes of two people: ^han Parker, who lived with him and bore two of his children (al- Ij V^ough, officially, they were never l^hjiarried) and trumpeter Red Rod- I I ney, both of whom were consult- J. .«nts on the film. Their Bird's-eye n view is the view the movie assumes. 1 i^rker's earlier wives - it's unclear I 1 just how many of them there were (Kl'cTiTd, more significantly, how many Jie was divorced from - are ignored, they're just not there. Neither, for that matter, are Lester Young, Jay f^McShann, Miles Davis, Buster .^-piith, and many, many other im- portant figures in the development iff one of the greatest musical geniuses of our century. There's a fictional alto player, called Buster J^ranklin, who is meant to stand for I something: he's the big megilah in msas City (and the protagonist, in *^he movie, of that cutting contest) *aTid he doesn't think much of the yjungBird. Later, he hears the ma- "Ture Charlie Parker (the film doesn't ^ ve us any idea of the intense V oodshedding Bird is said to have c )ne after that Kansas City fiasco) c. 'd is so upset by the greatness he hears (a little Salieri/Mozart here) he throw his horn in the river. At the end- of the film, Buster's a big rock and roll star, something that upsets Bird something awful - he attempts to steal Buster's new horn, presumably to send it, too, to sleep with the fishes also. It's a bit silly. The movie has two huge problems. One, it never gives us an idea of how important Charlie Parker was or of what a great musi- cal revolution bebop was. It never sets bebop up - we never see where it came from, never hear why it's dif- ferent, why it was so revolutionary. Also, we never see the huge social revolution it was - how the bebop- pers created their own language, style, and, most importantly, at- titude. The music in the film is ex- cellent - it's played by Bird, after all (although you can definitely tell that the alto solos are not as sonical- ly clear and forward as the rest of the music), but the film never shows you why Charlie Parker was, quite literally, worshipped. The other problem is a matter of context. It never sets the social stage, never gives us any hint, for example, why somebody like Char- lie Parker became a junkie when he was still a boy. It never shows us the social and economic realities of the '30s and '40s, never puts the drugs, the jazz life, the very essence of what became bebop (and what begat an entire generation of heroin-shooting jazz musicians) into focus. It doesn't try to. What made Charlie Parker great? The film doesn't tell us, maybe no film could. What made Charlie Parker? The film doesn't tell us that either, though it does strew vague artsy hints around. It's really the old Hollywood ver- sion of the artist again: a deeply- troubled alien in an uncaring, un- sympathetic, unartistic world. It's Kirk Douglas as Van Gogh, Gary Busey as Buddy Holly, Stacy Keach as Ernest Hemingway. Parker can't cope - of course he can't cope, he's an Artist, a Creator, a Genius, he shouldn't be expected to cope. And, in the end, the rest of the world is to blame for shutting its eyes, plugging its ears, and holding its nose. In a sense it's near the mark, but in a sense it's too simplistic. Bird is a good movie, I think - it's lovely to look at, filled with excellent perfor- mances, brimming with wonderful music, and very, very, very sincere. But the question of who was Char- lie Parker, and more importantly why was Charlie Parker, goes - after two-hours-and-forty-minutes - basically unanswered. 'j SUPREME SOVIETS - Jazz from the Soviet Union has been making itself heard over here over the past few years - what with Leo Records steadfastly documenting the avant-garde and Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs currently distributing some of Melodiya's albums locally. Well, Salt Lake City's The Space Agency, the folks who brought us the Ganelin Trio and The Leningrad Dixieland Band, are about to give us another couple of slices of Soviet jazz in the flesh. Ser- gei Kuryokhin, the extraordinary pianist, composer and all around jazz /pop /rock meshuganeh (he was the best part of Nam June Paik's recent PBS spectacle), will be spin- ning through Tucson (10/11), Chicago (10/14), Berkeley (10/21), Santa Cruz (10/23), New York's Knitting Factory (10/28 & 29, with John Zorn), Oberlin (11/6), the Knitting Factory again (11 /13), and Washington, DC (11/1 7&:1 8). Also Alexey Batashev, the Soviet Union's leading jazz critic, will be shepherding a group of Soviet all- stars around, concertizing (them) and lecturing (him). They are pianist Igor Brill, guitarist Alexey Kuznetsov, saxist Alexander Oseichuk, and bassist Victor Dvos- kin, and they will be in Washington (10/21), Colgate (10/28), Salt Lake City (11 /2), Provo (11 /3&4), Logan, UT (11/5), Quinnipac, NY (11/9), New York City (11/11 &:l2),and Bos- ton (11/13-16). In the meantime. Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs has just issued, on CD, Leonid Chizhik In Concert, by a wonderfully rhap- sodic solo pianist, and Jazz '84: Highlights From the IXth Moscow Jazz Festival, featuring an eclectic array of talent. Leo, not to be outdone, has sent us Sergei Kuryohkin's splendid and witty Pop Mechanics No. 17 and wild avant-garde vocalist Valentina Ponomareva's wild avant-garde Intrusion (not to mention new albums from American saxophonist Keshavan Maslak and Hungarian guitarist Sandor Szabo and percussionist Balazs Major, who do sort of a Hungary-meets-India thing). PD; Phillip David March, MD; Tony Fields, PD; Al B. Sure!; Marc Gunn, prod, dir.; Shawn Johnson, asst, promotions dir.; and Vincent Thomas, announcer. Tony Haynes: One Word = Songs In Minutes!! By Bob Long Tony Haynes is a 27 year old native of Southern California and for the past seven years has written songs for major artists like Robert Palmer, Earth, Wind & Fire, Quincy Jones, Al Jarreau, The Pointer Sisters, Philip Bailey, Stephanie Mills, George Duke, Robert Brookins and Jeffrey Osborne's recent #1 single "She's On The Left." During this period of Tony's career he has gained notoriety within his creative circle (his songs have sold over 12 million records and you can probably find one in every ten households in America) as the fastest spontaneous songwriter/poet in the music business today. Haynes says, "Give me a word and I can create a whole story around it that rhymes." I can personally attest to his ability to create songs/rhymes on the spot, having listened with amazement while he took words that I gave him and created songs. This man is truly amazing!! One of his goals is to make poetry a household word. He has written two books, one of modern poetry en- titled "Visions Of The Private Eye" and a book of romance entitled "Ships" which deals with relation- ships, courtships, hardships, ships that pass in the night, friendships, partnerships and companionships. Tony feels it's time for him to step out of the shadows and into the light of stardom. He wants to do what Nipsey Russell did with words and what Rod McKuen did with poems. He is doing what Smokey Robinson did to lyrics and is all set to do what LL Cool J does to rap. This young songwriter/enter- tainer/poet's act is innovative and funny with that certain something people find really entertaining. Tony Haynes aka The Private Eye says, 'Throughout the years I've learned that if you stick with something, believe in it and keep going for it, everything works out." For those A&R executives and producers who often need that last minute "hit" song to complete work on an LP, then let me tell you Tony Haynes is the man. Give him a word and he will give you a hit in minutes. TRACIE SIGNS IN - Capitol recording artist Trade Spencer greeted fans at a recent in-store appearance at Camelot Music in Charlotte, N.C. Spencer has just returned from an internation- al promotion tour in support of her self-titled debut album. Trade is shown autographing copies of her LP for two of her many fans. JAZZ ON JAZZ CASHB V DAY FOR A KING - Benny Carter (c) t^cently joined Roy Haynes and Bill iHarris in being named a Living National Juzz treasure at the Smithsonian Institution. Here, making the presentation to Carter, are Ka,SCAP president Morton Gould (1) and I Rep. John Conyers. R - I HAPSODY IN VIEW - There is something natural about the relationship be- tween jazz and film: both art forms are about 100 years old so there is very little jazz that hap- 'pened before there were films to ^document it. Tm not saying that - garly jazz is well documented on ^;lm - or, in fact, that any jazz is well 'documented on film - but there are films of Ellington in the '20s, little -ssiippets of Bix Beiderbecke, plen- ty of Fats Waller, Count Basie, things like that. , Bruce Ricker, the director of Last cf the Blue Devils and co-producer, “with Charlotte Zwerin, of the up- coming feature-length documen- iSiry Thelonious Monk: Straight, No Chaser (Zwerin is director and Clint ^Eastwood is executive producer), has a video company called Rhapsody ' Films, which has just issued some dine new videos, and is the co- programmer (with Bruce Gold- (j^tein) of an extraordinary three- week Jazz on Screen series set for JvJew York's Film Forum, October 21 - November 10. The Film Forum series brings .together some of the better jazz documentaries {Jazz On A Summer's J^ay, Blue Devils, television's The Sound of Jazz, Steve Lacy: Lift the Bandstand, the classic short Jammin' The Blues), some new films (notably ,'oird Now, a feature-length Charlie Parker documentary from Bel- liinm), and numerous fictional films i^ith jazz settings or soundtracks -iThe Gene Krupa Story, Round Mid- night, the neglected Absolute Begin- 'hSrs, with its Gil Evans score, J^levator to the Gallows, a rarely-seen jazz update of Othello called All .Njght Long). .^The complete schedule is as fol- lows: Jazz On A Summer's Day, in a new 35mm print /Elevator to the Gal- hwsljammin' The Blues, 10/21-23; ^lues In The Night/Orchestra Wives, 1 0/24; The Sound ofMiles Davis/Ab- solute Beginners/Steve Lacy: Lift the Bandstand, 10/25; Memories of Juke/A Brother With Perfect Timing about Abdullah Ibrahim), 10/26; Zhicago Blues/Blues For Central Avenue (about Ernie Andrews), 10/27; Art Blakey: The Jazz Mes- senger/ three shorts by Dick Fon- taine (on Sonny Rollins, Rahsaan Roland Kirk and Ornette Coleman), l0/28&:29; an evening of film clips from the extraordinary collection of the late David Chertok (to whom the series is dedicated), 10/30); The Sound OfJazz/All Night Long, 10/31 ; Round Midnight/Jazz in Exile, 11/1; Saxophone Colossus (on Sonny Rol- lins)/Mac/i/fo: A Latin Jazz Legacy/Sun Ra: A Joyful Noise, 11/2; Born To Swing/The Gene Krupa Story, 11 /3; an evening of clips from Ernie Smith's collection of jazz dance on film, 11/4; Bird Now/Eastwood (about the making of Bird), 11 /5&:6; Paris Blues/On The Road with Duke Ellington, 11/7; Mingus/Art Pepper: Notes From A Survivor, 11 /8; Ornette - Made in America/The Connection, 11/9; and The Last of the Blue Devils/The International Sweethearts ofRhythm/Tiny and Ruby: Hell Divin' Women, 11 /lO. It's a great, and fair- ly comprehensive, series. Videowise, Rhapsody has just released some of those same films on tape: A Brother With Perfect Timing, the leisurely stroll through Abdullah Ibrahim's music; Art Blakey: The Jazz Messenger, which gets to the heartbeat of one of jazz's great forces; the Fontaine shorts on Rahsaan and Ornette; the conten- tious and ornery Mingus, featuring Mingus, shotgun in hand, talking about his impending eviction and, surprise, the eviction itself; and Blues for Central Avenue, a good look at the neglected West Coast jazz scene of yore. Rhapsody has a number of the other films in the series out on home video, and they've also just released videos on George Crumb, Percy Mayfield, Chicago blues, and a percussion fes- tival. For a complete catalogue write to them at P.O. Box 179, New York, NY 10014. ' ^MEET THE MODERNS - New Or- j^iMns, the land of muffelettas and Mar- salises, has been getting an awful lot of attention, musically-speaking, these ^ I days. The great New Orleans R&B per- ^ ifr,rimers - like Irma Thomas, Ernie K- ' Johnny Adams and the like - are ^ 'iiiially getting wider play; a young New ^ Orleans conservative jazz scene - all I those fresh-faced NOCCA kids (the I many Marsalises, of course, Terence "I Blanchard, Donald Harrison, Harry :^C»nnick, Kent Jordan, etc.) - are wide- I ly^known; Cajun, blues, and all sorts of Jyi'ie^^her New Orleans sounds are getting 't-'l?.eard. Rounder Records has been in- |"^§irumental in helping this happen, thanks to its excellent "Modem New Or- Icii'ns Masters" series. But there is one of New Orleans music that, surpris- » I idgly, has been neglected: the thriving -(Contemporary jazz scene. Well it's '-’.eglected no longer. Rounder has had *the good sense to turn to Kalamu ya Salaam, the executive director of the Mew Orleans Cultural Foundation and i i Aa writer for that wonderful New Orleans ij I music monthly Wavelength, to produce a J I s-eries of albums called The New New Or- f 'eans Music, three volumes, each with two groups. They provide an excellent introduction to the contemporary players of the Crescent City. The three albums are New Music Jazz, avant-garde from The New Orleans Saxophone En- semble (Tony Dagradi, Earl Turbinton Jr., Fred Kemp, Roger Lewis) and The Improvisational Arts Quintet (Edward "Kidd" Jordan, Kent Jordan, Alvin Fielder, Clyde Kerr Jr., Elton Heron, Darryl Levine); Jump Jazz, with The Ed Frank Quintet (Frank, Fred Kemp, Wendell Brunious, Erving Charles, Smokey Johnson) and Ramsey McLean & The Survivors (McLean, Charles Neville, Charmaine Neville, Reggie Houston, Steve Masakowski, Herlin Riley); and Vocal Jazz with Germaine Bazzle & Friends (Alvin "Red" Tyler, Emile Vinette, George French, James Black) and Lady BJ & The Ellis Mar- salis Quartet (Marsalis, Victor Goines, Reginald Veal, Noel Kendrick). Many of the names will be familiar - some have left New Orleans and are playing around New York (Messrs. Riley and Veal are with Wynton Marsalis), others are already familiar to visitors to the an- nual New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Fes- tival (just six months away, folks!), others have experience going back to the '50s recordings of Fats Domino, Little Richard, and others. It's a good cross- section - from Kidd Jordan's free jazz to the vocalist's blues-tinged versions of jazz standards. Most of the music has a certain joie de musique common to the city, an ability to mix in fimk with bop with calypso with anything else. This is a unique project and it is helped by in- formative liner notes from producer Salaam. Rounder Records is taking care of business. 54TH ST. THEME - John Garcia Gensel is, without question, one of the most important figures on the New York jazz scene: he is the "Shepherd of the Night Hock," the minister to the jazz community. The Jazz Ministry at St. Peter's Lutheran Church has provided ecumenical services to jazz musicians forever and Gensel has been there - giving concerts, hanging out at concerts, presiding at funerals, nurturing and coimseling the jazz community. Now 71, Gensel is anticipating his retirement and so St. Peter's has begun a three-year fund-raising effort to provide an ap- prentice pastor to begin to take up Gensel's work. The first benefit concert will be an Oct. 27 gala salute to Lionel Hampton; he'll receive the Church's first Duke Ellington/Shepherd of the Night Flock Award and will jam with the likes of Stan Getz, Gerry Mulligan, Tito Puente, Bobby Short, Honi Coles and many, many others. It's a $25 ticket ($150 with a reception thrown in), St. Peter's is at Lexington Ave. and 54th St., and their number is (212) 935-2200. Without John Gensel, New York's jazz scene would be a poorer place, and this is a most important effor. Lee Jeske CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS Title, Artist, Label, Number. A MESSAGE IN THE MUSIC— few months ago, RJD Music of Las Vegas released one of the most entertaining records of the year, Somewhere Elvis Is Smiling by Gabriel. Recently I’ve received some additional RJD product and found it just as interesting. RJD is owned by Robert J. DiMaggio, a lesser-known member of a famous family and a talented individual in his own right. DiMaggio has written and produced "I’ll Love You Till The End of Time,” a pop ballad by a pair Vegas performers named Jerome Lopez and Diane Ellis. The com- bination of their two perfectly- groomed voices is reminiscent of Diana Ross and Lionel Ritchie on “Endless Love” and makes for a seamless adult/contemporary tune. But it’s another RJD album that has really captured my imagination. A couple years ago DiMaggio produced a record called A Special Tribute to America and now he is in- cluding it with every mail order of his other products (including the un- canny Elvis album.). The three lounge-ballads on this unabashed- ly open-hearted record are "Our Missing Children,” “So Please Give With Me” and "Peace on Earth.” Proceeds from the record go to sup- port a missing-children’s organiza- tion, a hospice in Las Vegas and the Veterans Fund of America. Hipsters like you and me might choke at this kind of selflessness, thinking these sentiments and this music are ex- fremely corny; but there’s a nation of people out there that instinctive- ly responds to the kind of altruism that Robert DiMaggio promotes with his time and money. He has sent copies of the album to Mr. and Mrs. Reagan, Sen. Paul Laxalt of Nevada and the Secretary of the United Nations—none of whom, I’m sure, believes a record requires irony to make its point. God bless you, Bob. Robert J. DiMaggio's special tribute to America, on RJD Records of Las Vegas, Nev. WHILE WE'RE OFF JAZZ - Fans of MPB (Brazilian popular music) have been feasting over the past couple of years, ana it doesn't seem to snow any signs of letting up. By a lovely coincidence two of the grand divas of "Tropacalia" are making rare New York appearances within 10 days of each other. Maria Bethania, the sultry-voiced sister of Caetano Velos, is making her long- awaited U.S. debut at Town Hall this Thursday and Friday (Nov. 3 & 4), a presentation of the Brazilian American Cultural Center, and Gal Costa, the highly-charged super- star whose dynamic show sold out Carnegie Hall a couple of years back, rolls into Avery Fisher Hall November 14 in a benefit for the Brazilian Cultural Foundation, with Portugese saxophonist Rao Kyao opening. MPB continues to inch forward in America. Bravo. BOPPING AROUND - Doesn't Billy Taylor have enough to do? We guess not. ON JAZZ 'ROUND MIDDAY - Dexter floats. ' T s AILING - There are lots of things you can do on a Caribbean cruise -- eat, lie in , I the sun, skeet shoot, eat, lie rin the sun, play volleyball, eat, lie in the sun, swim, etc. But in October on the NCUs flagship, the S.S. Nor- way (and, as of this year, the new M/S Seaward a week later), there's another option. The Thursday before last, for example, after I ate, I laid in the sun and ate some more, I wandered down to the ship's com- * fortable Saga Theatre for an after- noon "Saxophone Spectacular." Spectacular? Arnett Cobb, Buddy Tate, Illinois Jacquet, Flip Phillips, Benny Carter, Sam Rivers and Red . ^Holloway carving up 'jumpin' At -'n''^rhe Woodside"? Are you kidding? Avast, ye rmteysi! The S.S. Norway's Sixth Annual Floating Jazz Festival was a mainstream jazz fan's delight— a nifty encapsulation of jazz styles from swing to bebop (not a wide range, but the types of people who choose—and can afford-—cruises for their vacations are not likely to be your Art Ensemble of Chicago crowd). Hank O'Neal and Shelly Shier put the thing together every year and they know what they're doing, the musicians look and feel at home in the Norway's wide as- sortment of venues—along with the theatre, there are several nightclubs (Club Internationale, Checkers Cabaret, North Cape Lounge) that bring the cozy jazz club ambience to the open seas. And the musicians play with the kind of easy, relaxed feeling that comes to people who have spent their day eating, lying in the sun, eating and hanging out. Dexter Gordon was the ship's prime jazz celebrity and prime tease. Dexter was there as a guest— he hasn't played much in the past year and he wasn't there to play. But the "Dexter may show up with ( his horn" rumor kept things buzz- ’ ing for the week. On the last night, 1 after the Baked Alaskas had been paraded and eaten, Dexter—his tone intact but his strength ques- tionable—played "Now's the Time" with Clark Terry and a love- , ly "Stardust" with Tommy Flanagan. The music on board was excep- tional almost every step of the way. How could it not be? The players listed above don't need much kick- starting to get revved up and neither do guys like Kenny Davern, Red Rodney and Dizzy Gillespie. Dizzy came with his quintet (which - c- includes Sam Rivers), Jacquet brought his bruising big band, and young guitarist Frank Vignola led his New Quintet of the Hot Club of Fiance; but everybody else was teamai around three prime rhythm sections - Ray Bryant/Milt Hin- ton/Gus Johnson, John Bunch/Howard Alden/Michael Moore/Chuck Riggs, and Roger Kellaway/Major Holley/Ed Shaughnessy. There were week- long pairings - the two Reds (Rod- ney and Holloway), Hip Phillips and Kenny Davem - guys like Terry and Erskine Hawkins airing their big band charts in front of the Norway's own lickety-split or- chestra, and all sorts of jamming going on. The Texas Tenors - Cobb, Tate and jacquet - were ferocious at every turn; Gillespie got hot when Red Rodney blew some bebop steam In his face; Carter, Davem and Phillips were sublime. And, as an added bonus, gospel legend Marion Williams performed two uplifting sets, the second in tandem with Juanita Brooks, a big-voiced, sassy gospel/blues/jazz singer from New Orleans who, for her set, talked another passenger, Allen Toussaint, away from the blackjack tables and to the piano. The Norway's Hoating Jazz Fes- tival is, goodness knows, an expen- sive way to listen to jazz. But the jazz cruise costs no more than the regular cruises, so, in fact, if craising's your vacation choice, it can be a bargain. And the atmos- phere really can't be beat—-the structure of the Norway allows you to club hop; a band will do maybe two or three sets a night, alternating with another band, in one of two or three rooms. And the musicians are captive and relaxed—available for chitchat, bridge games, whatever else ship's passengers do with each other. There were three "Meet The Stars" bull sessions, a continuous, and very' well-programmed, jazz channel on the in-room televisions, and just enough jazz to make it at- tractive without surrounding you with it, without having it blot out the sun or drown out the lapping of the waves. (The lure of the islands was clearly not everybody's choice—at breakfast one morning, as we were about to get off the ship in St. Maarten, one guy grumbled that he didn't realize that the ship ever docked, he just thought he'd be able to sit on board and listen to live jazz all day every day.) The most amazing thing, from my standpoint, is that in all the lis- tening I did in my week on the Nor- way, 1 never - not once - heard anybody play "How Deep is the Ocean" or "My Ship.' And, remarkably, nobody played "St. Thomas," either before or after the ship docked in St. Thomas. Hmmm! Lee Jeske CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS 1 Title. Artist. Lal^el, Nimaber. JAZZ ON JAZZ SCORE! At a recent party to launch BMI's Jazz Composers Workshop BMI president and ceo Frances Preston (1) sang the praises of (l-r) Workshop musical directors Bob Brookmeyer and Manny Album and BMI director Burt Korall. RE: ISSUES I KNEW, ONE— The jazz reissue boom shows no sign of abating; jazz labels are spending more time in vaults these days than diamond dealers. It's a double-edged sword: Getting great music back into print is marvelous, but it does make it more difficult for contemporary musicians to get their music recorded. On the other hand, it does give contemporary musicians access to important music; music that will make them better musicians. In any case, Tm not complaining. Here's a quick recent label survey, part one of two (or possibly three). CAPITOL—Blue Note keep roll- ing along with one of the most steadfast reissue programs going. Out recently are CDs of eight pre- viously-reissued LPs (with extra CD material noted): Stanley Turrentine's That's Where It's At (one alternate take), Freddie Hubbard's Hub Cap (one alternate), Horace Silver's Finger' Poppin', Lee Morgan's Search For the New Land, Donald Byrd's Byrd in Hand, Grachan Moncur Ill's Evolution, Kenny Dorham's Trompeta Toccata, and Arthur Taylor's A.T.'s Delight. Just reissued for the first time, on CD, LP, and cassette, are Hank Mobley and Lee Morgan's Peckin' Time (with three alternates added to the CD), and Joe Henderson's Page One, classics both. At the same time. Blue Note has begun an admirable program for those who want to dip into some Blue Note classics but are in- timidated by the sheer number of them. Six "Best Of" albums, in all formats (with fewer tracks on the LPs) cover Dexter Gordon, Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Jimmy Smith, Horace Silver and Lee Mor- gan. Perfect Blue Note intros; per- fect stocking stuffers. As if all that wasn't enough, Capitol has also added another five Pacific Jazz reissues on CD. They are Gil Evans' classic Great Jazz Standards; Annie Ross and Zoot Sims' A Gasser! (a whole album and a bunch of other related stufO; Grand Enounter: 2 Degrees East 3 Degrees West, a '56 bicoastal band of John Lewis, Bill Perkins, Jim Hall, Percy Heath and Chico Hamilton; the Jim Hall Trio's (with Carl Perkins and Red Mitchell) Jazz Guitar (with an extra take), and Gerry Mulligan's California Con- certs Volume 2 (a lot of it previously unissued). EPIC—The good news is that Epic's Portrait series has finally yielded up its promised reissues. The bad news is that, information- wise, they're attempting to return us to the reissue dark ages. The good news, in all formats, are the tit- les: Louis Armstrong's Stardust, '30-32 sides, many of them master- pieces; Back Room Romp, '36-'39 recordings by four sets of Duke El- lington small bands, led by Rex Stewart, Barney Bigard, Johnny Hodges and Cootie Williams (talk about masterpieces!); Free For All, recordings by an early ('37) Artie Shaw Orchestra; Dave McKenna's rare '59 trio This is the Moment (showing McKenna to be a much better pianist today, not surprising- ly); and some terrific '36-'38 sides by Big Bill Broonzy, Big Bill's Blues. The bad news is that these albums contain liner notes and liner notes only: no personnel information, no recording dates, no recording loca- tions, no nothing. This is not just surprising, this is unheard of. Hey, Portrait, get with it, or at least tell your liner note writers that they're all we're going to get. A&M—This is perhaps the last label you'd expect jazz from but, in the words of senior vp David Stef- fen, "A&M's recent moves to be- come represented in virtually every area of music—from classical to children's, from Word to Windham Hill—could hardly be complete without jazz." No arguments here, Dave. John Snyder's in charge, the series is called A&M Jazz Heritage (eventually new recordings will be included) and it's culled from three places: early, sugary CTI, A&M's own meager jazz holdings, and Snyder's admirable '70s Horizon material.. The first nine CD-only reissues are Ornette Coleman's Dancing in Your Head (early Prime Time), Charlie Haden's Closeness (a minor classic, duets with Ornette, Keith Jarrett, Alice Coltrane and Paul Motian), Don Cherry's Brown Rice, Wes Montgomery's poppish Down Here On The Ground, Quincy Jones's Walking In Space, the Dave Brubeck Quartet's 25th Anniversary Reunion, Chet Baker's Don Sebes- ky-sweetened You Can't Go Home Again, and Gerry Mulligan's The Age of Steam. No extra tracks—just the albums as they were, in hand- some cardboard "digipaks" (a good alternative to jewel boxes) meticulously remastered by Snyder and jazz engineer extraordinaire Rudy Van GelHer.
